crop |>
  group_by(treatment, variety) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean = mean(yield_t_ha), median = median(yield_t_ha),
            sd = sd(yield_t_ha), iqr = IQR(yield_t_ha), .groups = "drop")

# A tibble: 6 × 7
  treatment variety     n  mean median    sd   iqr
  <chr>     <chr>   <int> <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1 Compost   A          10  3.72   3.74 0.450 0.673
2 Compost   B          10  3.95   3.86 0.339 0.567
3 Control   A          10  2.92   2.93 0.381 0.535
4 Control   B          10  3.32   3.34 0.518 0.498
5 Mineral   A          10  4.32   4.19 0.386 0.408
6 Mineral   B          10  4.39   4.35 0.302 0.312


Pooling groups can inflate spread because it combines between-group differences with within-group variation. Report the group definitions and sample sizes. Avoid presenting many decimal places beyond measurement precision.


7.11.6 Other averages: geometric and harmonic means
The arithmetic mean is not always the right average. When quantities multiply over time, such as growth ratios, the geometric mean is appropriate. When averaging rates over equal amounts of work, the harmonic mean is appropriate.
Suppose the area under a crop in a district grew by 10%, 20%, and 5% in three successive years. The growth factors are 1.10, 1.20, and 1.05. The average annual growth factor is their geometric mean, the cube root of their product, because applying it three times reproduces the total growth.

growth_factor <- c(1.10, 1.20, 1.05)
geometric_mean <- exp(mean(log(growth_factor)))
c(arithmetic = mean(growth_factor), geometric = geometric_mean)

arithmetic  geometric 
  1.116667   1.114947 

# Check: three years at the geometric mean give the same total growth
c(actual_total = prod(growth_factor), from_geometric = geometric_mean^3)

  actual_total from_geometric 
         1.386          1.386 


The arithmetic mean, about 1.117, overstates the average growth; the geometric mean, about 1.115, reproduces the actual total. Computing it as exp(mean(log(x))) avoids overflow with long series and works only for positive values.
A tractor ploughs three plots of 1 ha each at 0.4, 0.5, and 0.8 ha per hour. Its average rate over the 3 ha is the total area divided by the total time, which is the harmonic mean of the rates.

rate_ha_per_hour <- c(0.4, 0.5, 0.8)
harmonic_mean <- length(rate_ha_per_hour) / sum(1 / rate_ha_per_hour)
c(arithmetic = mean(rate_ha_per_hour), harmonic = harmonic_mean,
  total_area_over_total_time = 3 / sum(1 / rate_ha_per_hour))

                arithmetic                   harmonic 
                 0.5666667                  0.5217391 
total_area_over_total_time 
                 0.5217391 


The tractor spends longest on the slowest plot, so its true average rate, about 0.52 ha/h, is lower than the arithmetic mean of 0.57 ha/h. For any set of positive values that are not all equal, harmonic mean < geometric mean < arithmetic mean.


7.11.7 Percentiles and quantiles
The median is the 50th percentile; quartiles are the 25th and 75th. Any percentile can be calculated with quantile(). Percentiles answer questions such as “what yield did the best 10% of plots exceed?”

quantile(y, probs = c(0.10, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 0.90))

   10%    25%    50%    75%    90% 
2.8560 3.2725 3.8750 4.2200 4.4930 

top_10_threshold <- quantile(y, 0.90)
crop[crop$yield_t_ha >= top_10_threshold, c("plot_id", "treatment", "variety", "yield_t_ha")]

   plot_id treatment variety yield_t_ha
23    P023   Mineral       B       4.55
36    P036   Mineral       B       4.86
41    P041   Compost       A       4.52
45    P045   Mineral       A       5.16
46    P046   Mineral       A       4.72
47    P047   Mineral       B       4.84


R offers nine definitions of sample quantiles through the type argument; they differ slightly for small samples. The default (type = 7) is fine for description, but state it if exact values matter, because other software may use a different definition.


7.11.8 Shape: skewness and kurtosis
Two distributions can share a mean and SD but differ in shape. Skewness measures asymmetry: positive skewness means a long tail of large values, common in pest counts and weed biomass. Kurtosis describes how heavy the tails are relative to a normal distribution; excess kurtosis subtracts 3, so a normal distribution has excess kurtosis 0. Both can be calculated from moments about the mean.
\[g_1=\frac{m_3}{m_2^{3/2}},\qquad g_2=\frac{m_4}{m_2^{2}}-3,\qquad m_k=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i-\bar{x})^k\]

shape <- function(x) {
  x <- x[!is.na(x)]
  d <- x - mean(x)
  m2 <- mean(d^2); m3 <- mean(d^3); m4 <- mean(d^4)
  c(skewness = m3 / m2^1.5, excess_kurtosis = m4 / m2^2 - 3)
}
aphids <- read.csv("data/aphid_counts.csv")$aphids_per_plant
round(rbind(yield = shape(y), aphid_count = shape(aphids)), 2)

            skewness excess_kurtosis
yield          -0.29           -0.57
aphid_count     1.39            0.84

old <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
hist(y, main = "Plot yield", xlab = "t/ha", col = "#abc4e2")
hist(aphids, main = "Aphids per plant", xlab = "count", col = "#ebc276")







par(old)

The yields are close to symmetric, whereas the aphid counts are clearly right-skewed: most plants carry few aphids and a few carry many. For skewed data, the median and IQR summarize the centre and spread better than the mean and SD, and analyses may need a transformation (see Chapter 13). Different packages use slightly different small-sample corrections for these coefficients, so values can differ in the second decimal place. With small samples, skewness and kurtosis are very imprecise; always look at the histogram as well.


7.11.9 Comparing variability across characters
The coefficient of variation allows variability to be compared between characters measured in different units. Plant breeders, for instance, compare the variability of height, tiller number, and yield in a germplasm collection. Using the cleaned field book from Chapter 4:

fb <- read.csv("data/field_book_messy.csv", na.strings = c("", "NA", "n/a", "-"))
fb$plant_height_cm <- as.numeric(gsub(",", ".", fb$plant_height_cm))
fb$plant_height_cm[fb$plot == "P10"] <- 85.0       # documented correction
fb$grain_wt_g_plot[fb$plot == "P07"] <- 2430       # documented correction
traits <- fb[, c("plant_height_cm", "tillers", "grain_wt_g_plot")]
round(t(sapply(traits, function(x) c(
  n = sum(!is.na(x)), mean = mean(x, na.rm = TRUE), sd = sd(x, na.rm = TRUE),
  cv_percent = 100 * sd(x, na.rm = TRUE) / mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)))), 2)

                 n    mean     sd cv_percent
plant_height_cm 11   85.05   4.82       5.66
tillers         11   12.82   1.83      14.31
grain_wt_g_plot 12 2421.25 187.87       7.76


The SDs cannot be compared directly, because they are in centimetres, counts, and grams. The CVs show that tiller number is relatively the most variable of the three characters and plant height the least. As noted above, CV is meaningful only for ratio-scale variables with a true zero.


7.11.10 A descriptive statistics table for several variables
A single function can produce the complete descriptive table that reports and theses usually present.

describe <- function(x) {
  x <- x[!is.na(x)]
  n <- length(x)
  c(n = n, mean = mean(x), sd = sd(x), se = sd(x) / sqrt(n),
    cv_percent = 100 * sd(x) / mean(x), min = min(x), median = median(x),
    max = max(x), shape(x))
}
soil <- read.csv("data/soil.csv")
round(t(sapply(soil[, c("available_n_mg_kg", "available_p_mg_kg",
                        "available_k_mg_kg")], describe)), 2)

                   n   mean    sd   se cv_percent  min median   max skewness

available_p_mg_kg 60  18.75  6.48 0.84      34.53  8.2  19.15  29.4    -0.03
available_k_mg_kg 60 123.17 37.18 4.80      30.19 72.9 115.50 186.7     0.33
                  excess_kurtosis
available_n_mg_kg           -0.69
available_p_mg_kg           -1.31
available_k_mg_kg           -1.30


sapply() applies describe() to each column and t() turns the result so that each variable is a row. Report units in the table caption, round to a sensible precision for display, and state the number of missing values if any were removed.

title: 7  Describing agricultural variation
text:
7.13 Chapter Summary

Fill in the blanks
Answers are given at the end of the chapter.

The __________ is the middle value of ordered data.
The most frequently occurring value is the __________.
The __________ is the square root of the variance.
The coefficient of variation expresses the SD as a __________ of the mean.
The standard __________ measures the precision of a sample mean.
Sturges’ rule gives the number of __________ in a frequency table.
summary() returns the minimum, quartiles, median, mean and __________.
The argument na.rm = TRUE removes __________ values before a calculation.



Short-answer questions

Distinguish between the standard deviation and the standard error.
When is the median preferred to the mean?
Why is the CV useful for comparing the variability of different characters?
Describe the steps in constructing a grouped frequency distribution.
What does sapply() do?



Numerical and conceptual questions
Answers are given at the end of the chapter.

Find the mean, SD and CV of the yields 3.2, 3.8, 4.0, 3.5 and 4.6 t/ha.
A sample of 16 plants has SD 0.8 cm. Find the standard error of the mean.
How many classes does Sturges’ rule give for 150 observations?



Important formulae
Arithmetic mean:
\[
\bar x = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n x_i
\tag{7.1}\]
Sample standard deviation:
\[
s = \sqrt{\frac{\sum (x_i - \bar x)^2}{n-1}}
\tag{7.2}\]
Coefficient of variation:
\[
\text{CV} = \frac{s}{\bar x} \times 100
\tag{7.3}\]
Standard error of the mean:
\[
\text{SE}(\bar x) = \frac{s}{\sqrt n}
\tag{7.4}\]
Sturges’ rule for the number of classes:
\[
k = 1 + 3.322\log_{10} N
\tag{7.5}\]


Quick revision

Centre → mean, median, mode; spread → range, IQR, variance, SD, CV.
SD → spread of observations; SE → precision of the mean.
Skewed data or outliers → median and IQR.
Grouped frequency table → classes by Sturges’ rule, equal widths covering the whole range.
Missing values → na.rm = TRUE; always report the denominator.



Answers to fill in the blanks

1. median 2. mode 3. standard deviation 4. percentage 5. error 6. classes 7. maximum 8. missing



Solutions to numerical and conceptual questions

Mean \(=3.82\); SD \(=0.531\) (Equation 7.2); CV \(=0.531/3.82\times100 = 13.9\%\) (Equation 7.3).
By Equation 7.4, \(0.8/\sqrt{16} = 0.2\) cm.
By Equation 7.5, \(1 + 3.322\log_{10}150 = 8.23\), rounded up to 9.

8.2 Begin with a question and design
Our teaching question is: Which recorded characteristics are associated with differences in grain yield? The simulated trial has 60 plot records: five blocks, three management treatments, and two varieties with two replicate plots per combination. Nitrogen application is closely linked to management treatment. Thus, an association between nitrogen and yield may also reflect other treatment differences. Soil observations are linked by plot identifier.
EDA is a structured investigation of distributions, patterns, anomalies, and relationships. It generates and refines questions. Repeatedly searching for a small p-value and reporting only the successful test would give a misleading impression of evidence.

  theme_minimal()

Figure 8.2: Exploratory relationships in simulated observations; grouping is retained to reveal possible confounding.





These relationships need scientific interpretation. Does the predictor precede the response? Was it manipulated or only measured? Are measurements at the same spatial scale? In a real trial, assigning the same weather-station value to many plots does not create independent rainfall replicates. The teaching dataset varies plot-level water exposure for illustration; this must not be mistaken for many independent weather stations.

title: 8  An exploratory study of crop yield
text:
8.5 Write an EDA memo
An effective memo states the question, source and design, cleaning decisions, two or three supported patterns, and their limitations. For example: “Treatment-specific plots suggest differences in yield, with additional variation among blocks. Nitrogen and treatment are linked, so their separate effects cannot be inferred from a pooled scatter plot. A model should represent the experimental design before adding exploratory predictors.”
Do not invent numerical findings in prose. Extract values from your executed summaries and identify the relevant table or figure. Separate what the data show from what you propose as an explanation.

title: 8  An exploratory study of crop yield
section: 8.6 From an agricultural question to a sequence of comparisons
text:
8.6 From an agricultural question to a sequence of comparisons
A common difficulty in EDA is deciding where to begin. Students often calculate every available summary and draw several graphs, but cannot explain why each was needed. A more useful approach is to translate the question into a small sequence of comparisons.
For our yield question, begin with the response: is yield measured on the same basis for every plot? Next inspect treatment and variety balance. Then examine whether block differences are large enough to affect pooled comparisons. Finally examine measured predictors such as soil nitrogen. This order prevents a persuasive scatter plot from distracting us from an error in the underlying experimental table.

block_summary <- dat |>
  group_by(block) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean_yield = mean(yield_t_ha),
            lowest_yield = min(yield_t_ha), highest_yield = max(yield_t_ha),
            .groups = "drop")
block_summary

  block     n mean_yield lowest_yield highest_yield
  <int> <int>      <dbl>        <dbl>         <dbl>
1     1    12       3.47         2.4           4.3 
2     2    12       3.66         2.69          4.55
3     3    12       3.81         2.67          4.86
4     4    12       4.04         2.97          5.16
5     5    12       3.88         2.42          4.42

ggplot(dat, aes(factor(block), yield_t_ha, colour = treatment)) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = .12, height = 0, seed = 531)) +
  labs(x = "Block", y = "Grain yield (t/ha)", colour = "Treatment") +
  theme_minimal()








The table shows how many observations contribute to each block summary. The graph retains treatment information. If a block appears high-yielding, ask whether all its treatments tend to be higher or whether the pattern is driven by one treatment. An overall block mean alone cannot answer that second question.

title: 8  An exploratory study of crop yield
text:
8.7 Marginal patterns and conditional patterns
A marginal comparison combines observations over other variables. A conditional comparison examines a relationship within specified groups or after accounting for specified predictors. The distinction matters when varieties or management practices occur under different environmental conditions.
Imagine that improved seed is used mainly on irrigated farms and local seed mainly on rainfed farms. A marginal difference in yield between seed types includes differences in water availability. A graph stratified by irrigation status may reveal a smaller seed difference, a larger one, or even a reversal. This is a problem of the comparison being made, not a software malfunction.
In our simulated trial, treatment and nitrogen application are linked by construction. The following table makes that relationship visible before any regression is fitted.

dat |>
  group_by(treatment) |>
  summarise(mean_nitrogen = mean(nitrogen_kg_ha),
            minimum_nitrogen = min(nitrogen_kg_ha),
            maximum_nitrogen = max(nitrogen_kg_ha), .groups = "drop")

# A tibble: 3 × 4
  treatment mean_nitrogen minimum_nitrogen maximum_nitrogen
  <chr>             <dbl>            <dbl>            <dbl>
1 Compost            64.1             56.5             68.8
2 Control            24.3             10.2             30.6
3 Mineral            99.2             87.7            105  


If groups occupy largely separate nitrogen ranges, a model claiming to estimate a treatment effect “at the same nitrogen rate” may rely on comparisons with little support in the observed data. Including both variables in a formula does not automatically solve that lack of overlap. Describe it in the EDA memo so the eventual model is judged against the actual information available.
crumbs: 8  An exploratory study of crop yield

title: 8  An exploratory study of crop yield
text:
8.8 Recording exploratory decisions
Keep a short analysis diary. Record which patterns prompted a transformation, a subgroup comparison, or a proposed model. For example: “The initial histogram suggested a long upper tail, so I compared the original and logarithmic scales.” This is more transparent than presenting the final choice as if it had been specified before the observations were examined.
An exploratory plot may reveal an unexpected association worth studying. It is appropriate to report that observation as exploratory and propose a follow-up experiment. It is inappropriate to search many subsets, keep only the strongest association, and describe its ordinary p-value as though only one question had been asked.
There is also a difference between a data limitation and an analytical limitation. A missing weather-station identifier is a data limitation that may prevent assessment of clustering. Choosing not to fit a sophisticated model because it is beyond this course is an analytical boundary. State both clearly. A thoughtful descriptive conclusion is preferable to an inferential claim that the dataset cannot support.

Identify one apparent relationship that could be confounded and explain the mechanism.
Write a confirmatory question that would require a new experiment or independent dataset.
Explain why selecting only the five highest-yielding plots cannot identify the best management practice for all farms.

Chapter review. EDA is a disciplined way to learn from data and uncover design problems. It does not turn observational patterns into causal effects.

title: 9  Modelling crop growth
text:
9.1 Learning outcomes
Interpret logistic and Gompertz growth parameters, fit nonlinear models, assess residuals and parameter plausibility, and recognize the limits of extrapolation and repeated measurements.

title: 9  Modelling crop growth
section: 9.2 Why straight lines are often inadequate
text:
9.2 Why straight lines are often inadequate
During establishment a crop may accumulate little biomass; rapid growth follows, then growth slows as resources become limiting or maturity approaches. A straight line cannot represent all three phases. A sigmoid model describes an S-shaped trajectory using parameters that have biological interpretations.
Let \(W(t)\) denote biomass at time \(t\). One parameterization of the logistic curve is
\[W(t)=\frac{A}{1+\exp\{-k(t-t_i)\}}, \qquad A>0,\ k>0.\]
\(A\) is the asymptotic biomass, \(k\) controls the rate of approach, and \(t_i\) is the time of inflection. At \(t_i\), biomass is \(A/2\) and absolute growth rate is maximal at \(Ak/4\). The Gompertz form used here is
\[W(t)=A\exp\{-\exp[-k(t-t_i)]\}.\]
Its inflection occurs at biomass \(A/e\), and its maximum absolute growth rate is \(Ak/e\). Both have an upper asymptote, but the logistic is symmetric around its inflection whereas the Gompertz is asymmetric. Parameter meanings depend on the chosen formula; a package using other symbols may use a different parameterization.

title: 9  Modelling crop growth
text:
9.3 Understand the growth dataset
growth.csv contains simulated biomass in g/m² at 12 sampling times, with three independently harvested quadrats at each time. The independence assumption is part of this teaching design. Repeated measurements on the same plants require a model accounting for within-plant dependence, beyond ordinary independent-error nls().

growth <- read.csv("data/growth.csv")
plot(biomass_g_m2 ~ day, growth, pch = 19,
     xlab = "Days after sowing", ylab = "Biomass (g/m²)")







Figure 9.1: Simulated biomass measurements from independent quadrats sampled through time.





Before fitting, ask whether the observations span early growth, the inflection region, and a plateau. Without late observations the asymptote can be poorly identified even when the fitted curve looks convincing.

title: 9  Modelling crop growth
text:
9.4 Fit and compare curves
Nonlinear least squares chooses parameters that minimize the sum of squared residuals. Starting values guide its numerical search; they are not prior evidence. Here a plateau near 1,000 g/m², an inflection near day 50, and a positive growth rate are reasonable visual starting points.

logistic <- nls(biomass_g_m2 ~ A / (1 + exp(-k * (day - ti))),
                data = growth, start = list(A = 1000, k = .07, ti = 50),
                algorithm = "port", lower = c(A = 0, k = .0001, ti = -Inf))
gompertz <- nls(biomass_g_m2 ~ A * exp(-exp(-k * (day - ti))),
                data = growth, start = list(A = 1000, k = .06, ti = 45),
                algorithm = "port", lower = c(A = 0, k = .0001, ti = -Inf))
summary(logistic)


Formula: biomass_g_m2 ~ A/(1 + exp(-k * (day - ti)))

Parameters:

A  9.947e+02  5.477e+00  181.63   <2e-16 ***
k  7.477e-02  1.602e-03   46.68   <2e-16 ***
ti 5.006e+01  3.382e-01  148.03   <2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 15.71 on 33 degrees of freedom

coef(gompertz)

1039.1311376    0.0467095   42.2440535

grid <- data.frame(day = seq(min(growth$day), max(growth$day), length.out = 200))
plot(biomass_g_m2 ~ day, growth, pch = 19,
     xlab = "Days after sowing", ylab = "Biomass (g/m²)")
lines(grid$day, predict(logistic, grid), col = "#245A42", lwd = 2)
lines(grid$day, predict(gompertz, grid), col = "#B45C21", lwd = 2, lty = 2)
legend("topleft", c("Logistic", "Gompertz"),
       col = c("#245A42", "#B45C21"), lty = c(1, 2), bty = "n")








Compare AIC only for fits to the same response observations under comparable error assumptions. Lower AIC suggests a better balance of fit and complexity among the candidates; it does not prove biological truth. Do not compare raw-response and log-response AIC values without accounting for the transformed likelihood.

title: 9  Modelling crop growth
text:
9.5 Diagnostics and interpretation

old <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(fitted(logistic), residuals(logistic), pch = 19,
     xlab = "Fitted biomass", ylab = "Residual")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2)
qqnorm(residuals(logistic)); qqline(residuals(logistic))







par(old)
pars <- coef(logistic)
c(asymptote_g_m2 = pars[["A"]], inflection_day = pars[["ti"]],
  max_rate_g_m2_day = pars[["A"]] * pars[["k"]] / 4)

   asymptote_g_m2    inflection_day max_rate_g_m2_day 
        994.74260          50.05894          18.59469 


A curved residual pattern suggests a missing feature of the growth curve. Increasing residual spread suggests changing error variance. Check convergence, sensible parameter values, and sensitivity to starting values. Nonconvergence may reflect poor starting values, inadequate data coverage, or an unsuitable model; increasing iteration limits alone is not a scientific solution.
The curve predicts a mean trajectory, not a guaranteed individual observation. predict.nls() does not automatically provide valid confidence or prediction intervals from an interval argument as predict.lm() does. Uncertainty may require an appropriate bootstrap or another justified method. Avoid presenting an unqualified long-term biomass forecast from a short growth experiment.

title: 9  Modelling crop growth
section: 9.6 Seeing the role of each parameter
text:
9.6 Seeing the role of each parameter
It is easy to read a formula and still be unsure how its parameters affect the graph. Let us change one parameter at a time while keeping the others fixed. Begin with a logistic curve having an asymptote of 1,000 g/m², a rate parameter of 0.07 per day, and an inflection time of day 50.

logistic_curve <- function(t, A = 1000, k = .07, ti = 50) {
  A / (1 + exp(-k * (t - ti)))
}
t <- seq(0, 120, length.out = 200)
old <- par(mfrow = c(1, 3))
matplot(t, cbind(logistic_curve(t, A = 800), logistic_curve(t),
                logistic_curve(t, A = 1200)), type = "l", lty = 1,
        xlab = "Days", ylab = "Biomass (g/m²)", main = "Asymptote A")
matplot(t, cbind(logistic_curve(t, k = .04), logistic_curve(t),
                logistic_curve(t, k = .10)), type = "l", lty = 1,
        xlab = "Days", ylab = "Biomass (g/m²)", main = "Rate k")
matplot(t, cbind(logistic_curve(t, ti = 35), logistic_curve(t),
                logistic_curve(t, ti = 65)), type = "l", lty = 1,
        xlab = "Days", ylab = "Biomass (g/m²)", main = "Inflection time")







par(old)

Increasing A raises the upper plateau. Increasing k makes the transition from early growth to the plateau more rapid. Increasing ti moves the rapid-growth phase later in time. These changes can compensate for one another over a short observed interval, which explains why parameters may be unstable when observations do not cover the whole trajectory.
The logistic scale parameter used by R’s SSlogis() is another way of expressing the same curve. In its usual form, scal is 1/k. Thus a larger scal corresponds to a slower transition, whereas a larger k corresponds to a faster transition. Comparing printed parameter names without checking formulas can therefore reverse an interpretation.

title: 9  Modelling crop growth
text:
9.7 Absolute and relative growth rates
Absolute growth rate describes an increase in biomass per unit time. If biomass is in g/m² and time in days, its unit is g/m²/day. For the logistic curve, differentiating with respect to time gives
\[\frac{dW}{dt}=kW\left(1-\frac{W}{A}\right).\]
At small W, the factor 1 - W/A is close to one. As biomass approaches the asymptote, that factor approaches zero and absolute growth slows. Relative growth rate divides absolute growth by current biomass:
\[\frac{1}{W}\frac{dW}{dt}=k\left(1-\frac{W}{A}\right).\]
Its unit is per day. Relative growth can decrease even while the absolute amount accumulated each day is increasing. A small seedling adding 1 g to 2 g has a larger proportional increase than a large plant adding 10 g to 200 g, although the large plant adds more biomass in absolute terms.

predicted_w <- logistic_curve(t)
absolute_rate <- .07 * predicted_w * (1 - predicted_w / 1000)
relative_rate <- absolute_rate / predicted_w
head(data.frame(day = t, biomass = predicted_w,
                absolute_rate, relative_rate))

        day  biomass absolute_rate relative_rate
1 0.0000000 29.31223      1.991712    0.06794814
2 0.6030151 30.53742      2.072342    0.06786238
3 1.2060302 31.81215      2.156009    0.06777315
4 1.8090452 33.13827      2.242808    0.06768032
5 2.4120603 34.51769      2.332835    0.06758376
6 3.0150754 35.95240      2.426188    0.06748333


For sampled growth data, a finite difference (W2 - W1)/(t2 - t1) estimates an average absolute rate over an interval. It is not an exact instantaneous derivative. With destructive sampling, the two means come from different quadrats and both contribute uncertainty. Avoid interpreting differences between noisy individual observations as exact physiological rates.

title: 9  Modelling crop growth
section: 9.8 Choosing an error model is part of choosing a growth model
text:
9.8 Choosing an error model is part of choosing a growth model
Ordinary nonlinear least squares assumes that residual variation is additive on the response scale. A large plant and a small plant are then assumed to have the same residual variance. If variability grows in proportion to mean biomass, a logarithmic response or an explicitly modelled variance structure may be more appropriate. These choices change the statistical question.
Taking logarithms is possible only for positive values. It also changes how large discrepancies are weighted: a difference of 20 g is relatively substantial near 40 g and relatively small near 1,000 g. Do not fit on a transformed scale and then describe every back-transformed prediction as an unbiased arithmetic mean without considering the transformation.
When comparing curves, examine their behaviour over the measured interval, residual plots, parameter plausibility, and uncertainty. A nearly flat late-growth phase can support estimation of A; early observations alone cannot guarantee it. An agronomically unreasonable asymptote is a reason to reconsider coverage and model structure even if the numerical optimizer converged.

title: 9  Modelling crop growth
text:
9.9 A real-data extension
R’s Orange dataset records circumference repeatedly on five orange trees. It is useful for recognizing the difference between longitudinal observations and independent destructive samples.

data("Orange", package = "datasets")
head(Orange)

  Tree  age circumference
1    1  118            30
2    1  484            58
3    1  664            87
4    1 1004           115
5    1 1231           120
6    1 1372           142

with(Orange, interaction.plot(age, Tree, circumference,
                             xlab = "Age (days)", ylab = "Circumference (mm)"))








Read ?Orange before analysis. Fitting each tree separately can illustrate curve shapes; a population analysis should account for repeated measurements and differences among trees.

text:
9.10 Practical 9 and exercises

Fit both curves and tabulate their parameters, residual standard errors, and AIC values. Explain why their inflection biomasses differ.

Compare logistic growth parameters

Important formulae
Logistic growth model:
\[
W(t) = \frac{A}{1 + \exp\{-k(t - t_i)\}}
\tag{9.1}\]
Gompertz growth model:
\[
W(t) = A\exp\{-\exp[-k(t - t_i)]\}
\tag{9.2}\]
Absolute growth rate of the logistic model:
\[
\frac{dW}{dt} = kW\left(1 - \frac{W}{A}\right)
\tag{9.3}\]


Quick revision

S-shaped growth → logistic (symmetric) or Gompertz (asymmetric).
\(A\) → final size; \(k\) → rate; \(t_i\) → time of fastest growth.
Logistic maximum growth rate → \(kA/4\) at \(W = A/2\).
Compare fits by residuals, AIC and plausibility of parameters.
Do not extrapolate beyond the observed period.



Answers to fill in the blanks

1. S 2. inflection 3. asymptote 4. half 5. asymmetric 6. nls() 7. size 8. risky



Solutions to numerical and conceptual questions

By Equation 9.1, \(W(t_i) = A/2 = 10\) g.
From Equation 9.3 at \(W = A/2\): \(kA/4 = 0.15\times20/4 = 0.75\) g/day.
By Equation 9.2, \(W(t_i) = A/e = 7.36\) g.

title: 10  Agricultural time series and forecasting
text:
10.1 Learning outcomes
Construct a regular time series, distinguish trend from seasonality, calculate moving averages, fit an introductory ARIMA model, and evaluate forecasts using a chronological holdout and a baseline.
The detailed examples from the original time-series chapter are retained: English kings, monthly births, souvenir sales, and London rainfall. They teach time-series structure before the agricultural weather application. Local copies are supplied so a classroom render does not depend on a live download. These are historical series, not simulated agricultural observations. The data appendix records the original sources and units.
We will be using the following data to demonstrate Time series analysis in R. Download the data and save in your system for practice.
-kings.csv contains data on the age of death of successive kings of England, starting with William the Conqueror.
-births.csv is a data set of monthly births in New York City, in thousands, from January 1946 to December 1959 (originally collected by Newton).
-souvenir.csv contains monthly sales for a souvenir shop at a beach resort town in Queensland, Australia, for January 1987-December 1993.
-rain.csv data contains total annual rainfall in inches for London, from 1813-1912.

title: 10  Agricultural time series and forecasting
crumbs: 10  Agricultural time series and forecasting

title: 10  Agricultural time series and forecasting
text:
10.3 Plotting time series data
After importing a time series into R, the next step is often to create a plot of the data. You can do this using the plot.ts() function. For example, to plot the time series of the ages at death of 42 successive English kings, you would write:

plot.ts(kingsts)








In the time plot, the fluctuations in the data appear to be relatively consistent in size throughout the series. This suggests that an additive model could be appropriate for describing this time series. In an additive model, the components (trend, seasonality, and residuals) are added together, which works well when the variability (the size of fluctuations) does not change much over time.

plot.ts(birthsts)








The time series shows a pattern of seasonal variation in monthly births, with peaks in the summer and dips in the winter. This suggests that an additive model could be suitable, as the size of the seasonal fluctuations remains fairly constant and does not seem influenced by the overall level of the series. Additionally, the random variations in the data appear to stay relatively stable over time.

plot.ts(souvenirts)








In this case, an additive model doesn’t seem suitable because both the seasonal and random fluctuations increase as the time series level rises. To make the data more suitable for an additive model, we may need to apply a transformation. One common approach is to take the natural logarithm of the original data, which can help stabilize the variance and make the fluctuations more consistent across the series.

logsouvenirts <- log(souvenirts)
plot.ts(logsouvenirts)








In the log-transformed time series, the size of both the seasonal and random fluctuations appears relatively stable over time and does not seem to vary with the overall level of the series. This suggests that the log-transformed data is now more suitable for an additive model, as the fluctuations are more uniform throughout the time series.
crumbs: 10  Agricultural time series and forecasting

title: 10  Agricultural time series and forecasting
text:
10.4 Decomposing Time Series
Decomposing a time series involves breaking it down into distinct elements to better understand its underlying patterns. Typically, this process separates the data into three key components:

Trend Component: This reflects the long-term direction of the data, showing whether there is an overall upward or downward movement over time. It helps to identify the general course of the series without short-term fluctuations.
Seasonal Component: If the data exhibits regular patterns at consistent intervals, this component captures those repeating cycles. For example, monthly sales data may show higher sales during the holiday season every year. This helps to isolate predictable fluctuations from the rest of the data.
Irregular (or Residual) Component: After removing the trend and seasonal components, what’s left is the irregular component, which represents random noise or short-term variations that cannot be attributed to a clear pattern. These fluctuations are unpredictable and often occur due to unforeseen events or natural variability.

By decomposing a time series, you can better analyze and model the individual components, making it easier to forecast future values or understand the underlying behaviors of the data.

10.4.1 Decomposing Non-Seasonal Data
A non-seasonal time series typically consists of a trend component and an irregular component. Decomposing this type of time series involves estimating these two components separately.
To estimate the trend component of a non-seasonal time series that can be modeled using an additive approach, a common technique is to apply a smoothing method. One effective method for this is the simple moving average (SMA), which helps to smooth out short-term fluctuations and highlight longer-term trends.
In R, you can use the SMA() function from the “TTR” package to calculate the simple moving average of your time series data. Here is how to do it:

Install the “TTR” Package: If you haven’t already installed the “TTR” package, you can do so by running the following command in R:


install.packages("TTR")


Load the “TTR” Package: Once the package is installed, you can load it into your R session with the following command:


library(TTR)

After loading the package, you can then use the SMA() function to compute the simple moving average and obtain the trend component of your non-seasonal time series. This process allows you to better understand the underlying trend in the data by reducing noise from irregular fluctuations.

kingstsSMA3 <- SMA(kingsts,n=3)
plot.ts(kingstsSMA3)








Although smoothing the time series with a simple moving average of order 3 has helped reduce some fluctuations, there are still considerable random variations present. To achieve a more accurate estimation of the trend component, it may be beneficial to apply a higher-order moving average.
Finding the optimal level of smoothing often requires some trial and error to determine the best order that balances noise reduction while preserving the essential patterns in the data.
For instance, you can experiment with a simple moving average of order 8 to see if this provides a clearer representation of the trend. Here’s how you can do that in R:

kingstsSMA8 <- SMA(kingsts,n=8)
plot.ts(kingstsSMA8)








Using a higher order like 8 should help smooth the data further, potentially reducing the random fluctuations and allowing for a clearer view of the underlying trend. This iterative approach can lead to a more accurate understanding of the time series behavior.


10.4.2 Decomposing Seasonal Data
A seasonal time series is characterized by three components: a trend component, a seasonal component, and an irregular component. Decomposing this time series involves separating it into these three distinct elements to better understand its structure.
To estimate the trend and seasonal components of a seasonal time series that can be modeled using an additive approach, you can utilize the decompose() function in R. This function effectively breaks down the time series into its constituent components, providing estimates for each.
Here’s how to use the decompose() function:

Apply the decompose() Function: You can call this function on your seasonal time series object. For example:


birthstscomp <- decompose(birthsts)


Accessing Components: The decompose() function returns a list object containing the estimates of the seasonal, trend, and irregular components. You can access these components using the following names:

birthstscomp$seasonal: This element holds the estimated seasonal component.
birthstscomp$trend: This contains the estimated trend component.
birthstscomp$random: This represents the irregular component.


By decomposing the time series, you can analyze each component separately, which can enhance your understanding of the data and improve forecasting accuracy.
Inspect the twelve seasonal factors returned by the decomposition. Their scale is thousands of births. Positive factors identify months above the estimated trend and negative factors identify months below it; compare tapply(birthstscomp$seasonal, cycle(birthsts), mean) rather than relying on a remembered month or value.
To visualize these components (trend, seasonal and irregular), you can use the plot() function in R. Here is how to do it:

Plot the Components: After decomposing your time series, you can create plots for each component as follows:


plot(birthstscomp)








This command will generate a series of plots showing the estimated trend, seasonal, and irregular components of your time series, allowing you to analyze and interpret the behavior of each component visually.
The plot presented above displays the original time series at the top, followed by the estimated trend component, the estimated seasonal component, and finally, the estimated irregular component at the bottom. The trend component reveals a slight decline from approximately 24 in 1947 to around 22 in 1948. After this dip, there is a consistent upward trend, reaching about 27 by 1959.

10.5 Seasonally Adjusting a Time Series
Seasonal adjustment of a time series involves removing the seasonal effects to reveal the underlying trends and irregularities more clearly. If the time series can be described using an additive model, this process is relatively straightforward. By estimating the seasonal component and subtracting it from the original data, you can remove the seasonal variation and obtain a seasonally adjusted time series.
Here’s how to achieve this in R using the decompose() function:

Estimate the Seasonal Component: First, decompose the time series to estimate its seasonal component using the decompose() function. This function calculates the seasonal, trend, and irregular components of the data.


birthstscomp<- decompose(birthsts)


Subtract the Seasonal Component: Once you have the seasonal component, subtract it from the original time series to remove the seasonality. This gives you a seasonally adjusted series:


birthstsadj<- birthsts - birthstscomp$seasonal


Interpretation: The result is a time series without the repetitive seasonal fluctuations, making it easier to focus on trends and irregular components. For example, if you’re analyzing the number of births per month in New York City, this adjustment will help you see whether the overall trend in births is increasing or decreasing, without being influenced by regular seasonal peaks and troughs.

By seasonally adjusting the data, analysts can make more accurate comparisons and forecasts without seasonal noise. This process is crucial in understanding the true underlying behavior of time series data, especially when making decisions based on long-term trends.
We can then plot the seasonally adjusted time series using the plot() function

plot(birthstsadj)

10.6 Forecasts Using Exponential Smoothing
Exponential smoothing, first introduced by Robert Goodell Brown in 1956 and later refined by Charles C. Holt in 1957, is a widely effective technique for smoothing time-series data. Unlike methods like the simple moving average, which apply equal weights to past data points, exponential smoothing uses an exponentially decreasing weight function. This approach assigns more significance to recent observations and less to older ones. A key parameter in this method is the smoothing constant, which determines the rate of decay for the weights. Due to its straightforward nature and ease of application, exponential smoothing is frequently employed in time-series analysis, often incorporating factors like seasonality based on user-defined assumptions.
Exponential smoothing is generally used to make short term forecasts, but longer-term forecasts using this technique can be quite unreliable.
When the smoothing factor (α) is larger, the level of smoothing decreases. An α value close to 1 results in less smoothing, giving more weight to recent changes in the data. Conversely, an α value closer to 0 leads to greater smoothing, making the model less responsive to recent fluctuations.
There is no single alpha value suitable for every series; estimation and forecast evaluation are needed. In some cases, the statistician’s expertise is used to choose an appropriate factor. Alternatively, statistical methods can be applied to optimize α, such as using the least squares method to find the value that minimizes the sum of errors in the model.

10.6.1 Types of Exponential Smoothing
1. Simple exponential smoothing: for series with no trend and no seasonality.
\[F_{t+1} = \alpha Y_t + (1 - \alpha) F_t\]
where \(F_{t+1}\) is the forecast for the next period, \(Y_t\) the observation at time \(t\) and \(F_t\) the forecast for time \(t\). Repeated substitution shows that the weight on the observation \(j\) periods ago is \(\alpha(1-\alpha)^j\).
2. Holt’s linear (trend) method: for series with a trend but no seasonality. It has a level \(\ell_t\) with smoothing constant \(\alpha\), and a slope \(b_t\) with smoothing constant \(\beta\):
\[\ell_t = \alpha Y_t + (1 - \alpha)(\ell_{t-1} + b_{t-1})\] \[b_t = \beta(\ell_t - \ell_{t-1}) + (1 - \beta) b_{t-1}\] \[F_{t+h} = \ell_t + h\,b_t\]
3. Holt–Winters method: for series with trend and seasonality of period \(m\), with a third smoothing constant \(\gamma\) for the seasonal component \(s_t\).
Additive seasonality (seasonal swings of constant size):
\[\ell_t = \alpha (Y_t - s_{t-m}) + (1 - \alpha)(\ell_{t-1} + b_{t-1})\] \[b_t = \beta(\ell_t - \ell_{t-1}) + (1 - \beta) b_{t-1}\] \[s_t = \gamma (Y_t - \ell_t) + (1 - \gamma) s_{t-m}\] \[F_{t+h} = \ell_t + h\,b_t + s_{t+h-m}\]
Multiplicative seasonality (seasonal swings proportional to the level):
\[\ell_t = \alpha \frac{Y_t}{s_{t-m}} + (1 - \alpha)(\ell_{t-1} + b_{t-1})\] \[b_t = \beta(\ell_t - \ell_{t-1}) + (1 - \beta) b_{t-1}\] \[s_t = \gamma \frac{Y_t}{\ell_t} + (1 - \gamma) s_{t-m}\] \[F_{t+h} = (\ell_t + h\,b_t)\, s_{t+h-m}\]
In the forecast equations, \(s_{t+h-m}\) is the most recent estimate of the seasonal effect for the season being forecast (for \(h > m\), use \(s_{t+h-km}\) with \(k\) the smallest integer such that \(h \le km\)).
All three methods are fitted with HoltWinters(): set gamma = FALSE for Holt’s method, and both beta = FALSE, gamma = FALSE for simple exponential smoothing. Use seasonal = "multiplicative" for multiplicative Holt–Winters.


10.6.2 Advantages of Exponential Smoothing

Simplicity: It is relatively easy to implement and understand.
Flexibility: Different types can accommodate various data patterns (trends and seasonality).
Adaptability: The method can quickly adjust to changes in the data patterns.

Exponential smoothing is a powerful technique for forecasting time series data. By applying weighted averages to past observations, it effectively captures trends and seasonal patterns, making it a valuable tool for analysts and decision-makers. The method’s adaptability and ease of use make it an essential part of any forecasting toolkit.
Consider the data rain.csv

rainseries <- ts(rain,start=c(1813))
plot.ts(rainseries)








In the above plot we can observe that the mean remains approximately constant at around 25 inches, and the random fluctuations appear to be relatively stable over time. Given this, it seems appropriate to apply an additive model for the time series. Consequently, we can generate forecasts using simple exponential smoothing.
In R, we can fit a simple exponential smoothing model using the HoltWinters() function. For simple exponential smoothing, we must set the parameters beta = FALSE and gamma = FALSE, as these parameters are utilized for Holt’s or Holt-Winters exponential smoothing.
The HoltWinters() function returns a list containing several key components. To forecast a time series, such as London’s annual rainfall, with simple exponential smoothing, we would use the following R code:

rainforecast <-HoltWinters(rainseries, beta = FALSE, gamma = FALSE)
rainforecast

10.7 Holt, Holt–Winters and ARIMA forecasting
The simple exponential smoothing model above is the first of a family of forecasting methods. This section completes the family with forecasts beyond the data, checks of the forecast errors, Holt’s and Holt–Winters methods, and ARIMA models (R. J. Hyndman and Athanasopoulos 2021).

10.7.1 Forecasting future values
Forecasts beyond the data are made with forecast() from the forecast package (R. Hyndman et al. 2023). Here we forecast rainfall for 1913–1920 (8 years):

library(forecast)
rainforecast8 <- forecast(rainforecast, h = 8)
rainforecast8

     Point Forecast    Lo 80    Hi 80    Lo 95    Hi 95
1913       24.67819 19.17493 30.18145 16.26169 33.09470
1914       24.67819 19.17333 30.18305 16.25924 33.09715
1915       24.67819 19.17173 30.18465 16.25679 33.09960
1916       24.67819 19.17013 30.18625 16.25434 33.10204
1917       24.67819 19.16853 30.18785 16.25190 33.10449
1918       24.67819 19.16694 30.18945 16.24945 33.10694
1919       24.67819 19.16534 30.19105 16.24701 33.10938
1920       24.67819 19.16374 30.19265 16.24456 33.11182

plot(rainforecast8)








The point forecast is 24.68 inches for every year, with 80% and 95% prediction intervals (the dark and light shaded bands).


10.7.2 Checking the forecast errors
If the model is adequate, the forecast errors (residuals) should show no autocorrelation, have constant variance and be roughly normally distributed with mean zero. The autocorrelation function (ACF) and the Ljung–Box test check the first condition:

res <- na.omit(residuals(rainforecast8))
acf(res, lag.max = 20)







Box.test(res, lag = 20, type = "Ljung-Box")


    Box-Ljung test

data:  res
X-squared = 17.401, df = 20, p-value = 0.6268


No autocorrelation falls outside the significance bounds except by chance, and the Ljung–Box test is not significant (p ≈ 0.63). There is therefore little evidence of autocorrelation in the forecast errors, and simple exponential smoothing provides an adequate forecasting model for London rainfall.

hist(res, breaks = 15, freq = FALSE, col = "grey90", main = "Forecast errors")
curve(dnorm(x, mean(res), sd(res)), add = TRUE, col = "red", lwd = 2)










10.7.3 Holt’s exponential smoothing
For a series with a trend but no seasonality we use Holt’s method. The built-in airmiles data give the annual revenue passenger miles flown by US commercial airlines, 1937–1960, which has a strong upward trend:

plot(airmiles, ylab = "Passenger miles (thousands)")







airholt <- HoltWinters(airmiles, gamma = FALSE)
airholt

10.7.5 ARIMA models
Exponential smoothing makes no assumption about correlation between successive values. ARIMA (autoregressive integrated moving average) models describe that correlation explicitly. An ARIMA(\(p,d,q\)) model has \(p\) autoregressive terms, \(d\) differences and \(q\) moving-average terms; seasonal ARIMA models add seasonal terms ARIMA(\(P,D,Q\))\(_m\).
The orders can be chosen by examining the ACF and partial ACF of the differenced series, or automatically with auto.arima(), which compares candidate models by AICc:

kingsarima <- auto.arima(kingsts)
kingsarima

Series: kingsts 
ARIMA(0,1,1) 

Coefficients:

      -0.7218

AIC=344.13   AICc=344.44   BIC=347.56

10.8 Agricultural applications, interpretation, and further practice

10.8.1 Time order carries information
Monthly rainfall, weekly pest counts, and annual crop yields are time series when observations have a meaningful chronological order. Nearby observations may be correlated. A random train/test split can leak future information into an analysis and exaggerate forecast accuracy.
A trend is a sustained change in level. Seasonality is a recurring pattern at a known period, such as 12 months. Irregular variation remains after systematic components are described. An additive representation is \(Y_t=T_t+S_t+E_t\). A multiplicative representation is more plausible when fluctuations increase with the series level, and may motivate a logarithmic transformation for strictly positive values.


10.8.2 Create and inspect a regular series

weather <- read.csv("data/weather.csv")
weather$date <- as.Date(weather$date)
weather <- weather[order(weather$date), ]
expected <- seq(as.Date("2015-01-01"), as.Date("2024-12-01"), by = "month")
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(weather$date), identical(weather$date, expected),
          all(is.finite(weather$rain_mm)))
rain <- ts(weather$rain_mm, start = c(2015, 1), frequency = 12)
plot(rain, ylab = "Monthly rainfall (mm)", xlab = "Year")







monthplot(rain, ylab = "Monthly rainfall (mm)", xlab = "Month")








frequency = 12 declares 12 equally spaced observations per seasonal cycle; it does not fill gaps or verify dates. Irregular or missing months must be investigated before constructing the series. The simulation is smooth and complete for teaching; real rainfall often has zeros, skewness, extreme events, and structural changes.


10.8.3 Moving averages and decomposition

trailing3 <- stats::filter(rain, rep(1 / 3, 3), sides = 1)
plot(rain, col = "grey60", ylab = "Monthly rainfall (mm)")
lines(trailing3, col = "#245A42", lwd = 2)







decomposition <- stl(rain, s.window = "periodic")
plot(decomposition)








A trailing three-month average uses the current and previous two months. A centred average also uses future observations relative to its centre, so it is suitable for retrospective description but not directly available at a forecast origin. Larger windows smooth more but can hide rapid changes. stl() here assumes a fixed seasonal pattern through s.window = "periodic"; inspect whether that is reasonable.


10.8.4 ARIMA as a starting model
ARIMA combines autoregression (dependence on past values), differencing (changes between successive values), and moving-average error terms (dependence on past shocks). The notation ARIMA\((p,d,q)\) gives their orders. Seasonal terms have analogous orders and a seasonal period. The moving-average term in ARIMA is not the same as a simple rolling mean of observations.
Automatic selection searches candidate models under an information criterion. It cannot determine whether a forecast is useful for an agricultural decision. Fit only on the training period and compare predictions with a simple alternative.

library(forecast)
train <- window(rain, end = c(2022, 12))
test <- window(rain, start = c(2023, 1))
fit <- auto.arima(train, seasonal = TRUE, stepwise = FALSE, approximation = FALSE)
fit

10.8.5 Check residuals and communicate uncertainty

checkresiduals(fit)









    Ljung-Box test

data:  Residuals from ARIMA(0,0,0)(0,1,1)[12] with drift
Q* = 18.591, df = 18, p-value = 0.4174

Model df: 1.   Total lags used: 19


The residual time plot reveals changing spread or isolated shocks; the autocorrelation function identifies remaining temporal patterns; and a Ljung–Box test checks a set of residual autocorrelations. A large p-value does not prove independence. A good forecast should also be plausible: an unconstrained Gaussian model may generate negative rainfall predictions. Consider suitable transformations or nonnegative models rather than silently replacing negative forecasts with zero.
Prediction intervals describe uncertain future observations under the model. They do not guarantee that all future values lie inside them. Changes in climate, instrumentation, or management can invalidate historical relationships.
After choosing a method using training and validation, refit it on all available historical data for an operational forecast. Keep the evaluation results separate from this final fit.

10.9 Live R laboratory

Smooth a seasonal series and forecast
Edit the code, then select Run R. The first run downloads R into your browser and may take a little time. Copy code also lets you use this example in RStudio.
set.seed(531)
month <- 1:60
rain <- ts(100 + 0.3 * month + 30 * sin(2 * pi * month / 12) +
           rnorm(60, 0, 8), start = c(2020, 1), frequency = 12)
smooth <- stats::filter(rain, rep(1/12, 12), sides = 2)
plot(rain, col = "#386ca2", ylab = "Simulated rain (mm)")
lines(smooth, col = "#b87521", lwd = 3)
fit <- arima(rain, order = c(1, 0, 0),
             seasonal = list(order = c(1, 0, 0), period = 12))
predict(fit, n.ahead = 3)
Investigate. The forecast prints predictions and standard errors. This is a model demonstration on simulated rainfall, not an operational weather forecast. Explain why smoothing produces missing values at the ends.







From the browser to your practical notebook



Record the input you changed, the output you obtained, and your interpretation. These live examples use base R and work independently. The full chapter examples, including package-based analyses, remain available with copy buttons for RStudio. Browser objects last until this page is reloaded; Reset code restores the editor text. Internet access is needed on first use; long or interactive desktop tasks belong in RStudio.








Historical Insights



Charles C. Holt developed exponential smoothing with trends in 1957 and his student Peter R. Winters added seasonality in 1960. George Box and Gwilym Jenkins published the ARIMA methodology in Time Series Analysis: Forecasting and Control in 1970.

title: 10  Agricultural time series and forecasting
text:
10.10 Chapter Summary

Fill in the blanks
Answers are given at the end of the chapter.

A time series is stored in R with the function __________.
For monthly data the frequency argument is __________.
The long-term movement of a series is its __________.
A pattern that repeats every year is the __________ component.
decompose() estimates the trend with a centred __________ average.
In simple exponential smoothing, an \(\alpha\) close to 0 gives __________ smoothing.
Holt’s method adds a smoothing constant \(\beta\) for the __________.
The Ljung–Box test checks the forecast errors for __________.



Short-answer questions

Distinguish between additive and multiplicative time series models.
How is a series seasonally adjusted?
Interpret an estimated \(\alpha\) of 0.02 in simple exponential smoothing.
When would you use Holt–Winters rather than Holt’s method?
What should the residuals of a good forecasting model look like?



Numerical and conceptual questions
Answers are given at the end of the chapter.

The current forecast is 24 and the new observation 30. With \(\alpha = 0.2\), find the next forecast.
Holt’s method gives level 100 and slope 5 at time \(t\). Forecast 3 periods ahead.
An additive series has the value 30 in July, when the seasonal effect is +2.5. Find the seasonally adjusted value.



Important formulae
Simple exponential smoothing:
\[
F_{t+1} = \alpha Y_t + (1-\alpha)F_t
\tag{10.1}\]
Holt’s forecast \(h\) periods ahead:
\[
F_{t+h} = \ell_t + h\,b_t
\tag{10.2}\]
Additive decomposition and seasonal adjustment:
\[
Y_t = T_t + S_t + I_t, \qquad Y_t^{\text{adj}} = Y_t - S_t
\tag{10.3}\]


Quick revision

Plot first; constant fluctuations → additive; growing fluctuations → log or multiplicative.
decompose() → trend, seasonal, irregular; adjust by subtracting \(S_t\).
No trend, no season → simple smoothing; trend → Holt; trend and season → Holt–Winters.
\(\alpha\) near 1 → follows recent data; \(\alpha\) near 0 → long-run average.
Check residuals: no autocorrelation, constant variance.



Answers to fill in the blanks

1. ts() 2. 12 3. trend 4. seasonal 5. moving 6. heavy 7. trend 8. autocorrelation



Solutions to numerical and conceptual questions

By Equation 10.1, \(0.2\times30 + 0.8\times24 = 25.2\).
By Equation 10.2, \(100 + 3\times5 = 115\).
By Equation 10.3, \(30 - 2.5 = 27.5\).





Hyndman, Rob J., and George Athanasopoulos. 2021. Forecasting: Principles and Practice. 3rd ed. Melbourne: OTexts. https://otexts.com/fpp3/.


Hyndman, Rob, George Athanasopoulos, Christoph Bergmeir, Gabriel Caceres, Leanne Chhay, Kirill Kuroptev, Mitchell O’Hara-Wild, et al. 2023. Forecast: Forecasting Functions for Time Series and Linear Models. https://pkg.robjhyndman.com/forecast/.

title: 11  Hypothesis tests and confidence intervals
text:
11.1 Learning outcomes
Translate an agricultural question into a null and alternative hypothesis, select an independent or paired t-test, check its assumptions, test proportions and Mendelian ratios, analyze a contingency table, use rank-based alternatives when appropriate, and interpret effect sizes, intervals, and p-values.
crumbs: 11  Hypothesis tests and confidence intervals

title: 11  Hypothesis tests and confidence intervals
text:
11.2 From description to inference
Descriptive statistics summarize observed data. Inference uses a sampling or randomization model to reason about an unobserved population or treatment effect. The experimental unit is the smallest unit independently assigned a treatment. Five leaves measured on each of four treated plants do not create twenty independently treated plants.
A null hypothesis specifies a reference claim, such as zero difference in population means. A test statistic measures discrepancy from that claim relative to sampling variation. A p-value is the probability, under the null model and its assumptions, of a test statistic at least as extreme as the observed one. It is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true, nor the probability that a result will replicate.
Choose the significance level and primary question before inspecting outcomes. Report an estimated effect and an interval alongside the p-value. Statistical significance does not imply agricultural or economic importance. Failure to reject is not proof of equality.
crumbs: 11  Hypothesis tests and confidence intervals

title: 11  Hypothesis tests and confidence intervals
section: 11.3 Worked example: uncertainty in a mean
text:
11.3 Worked example: uncertainty in a mean
For independent observations with unknown population variance, a two-sided confidence interval for a population mean is
\[\bar{x}\ \pm\ t_{1-\alpha/2,n-1}\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}.\]
The critical value comes from a Student t distribution with n - 1 degrees of freedom. It is larger than the normal critical value when the sample is small, reflecting additional uncertainty in estimating the variance.

y <- c(4.2, 4.8, 5.1, 4.5)
se <- sd(y) / sqrt(length(y))
critical <- qt(.975, df = length(y) - 1)
c(mean = mean(y), se = se, lower = mean(y) - critical * se,
  upper = mean(y) + critical * se)

     mean        se     lower     upper 
4.6500000 0.1936492 4.0337219 5.2662781 

t.test(y)$conf.int

[1] 4.033722 5.266278
attr(,"conf.level")
[1] 0.95


The interval is approximately 4.03 to 5.27 t/ha. It estimates a population mean under the sampling assumptions; it is not an interval containing 95% of individual plot yields. Four conveniently selected plots would not justify population inference merely because the formula can be evaluated.
For a two-sample comparison, the same principle estimates a difference and its standard error. Welch’s method estimates variance contributions separately and adjusts the reference degrees of freedom. For a paired comparison, apply the one-sample idea to within-pair differences.
crumbs: 11  Hypothesis tests and confidence intervals

title: 11  Hypothesis tests and confidence intervals
text:
11.4 One-sample and two-sample t-tests
PlantGrowth is a real dataset supplied with R containing dry-weight measurements for a control and two treatment groups. The documentation does not identify the treatments as fertilizer rates, so do not invent that interpretation.

data("PlantGrowth", package = "datasets")
aggregate(weight ~ group, PlantGrowth, function(x) c(n = length(x), mean = mean(x), sd = sd(x)))

  group   weight.n weight.mean  weight.sd
1  ctrl 10.0000000   5.0320000  0.5830914
2  trt1 10.0000000   4.6610000  0.7936757
3  trt2 10.0000000   5.5260000  0.4425733

control <- subset(PlantGrowth, group == "ctrl")$weight
t.test(control, mu = 5)


    One Sample t-test

data:  control
t = 0.17355, df = 9, p-value = 0.8661
alternative hypothesis: true mean is not equal to 5
95 percent confidence interval:
 4.614882 5.449118
sample estimates:
mean of x 
    5.032 


The one-sample example asks whether the population mean control weight differs from 5 in the dataset’s measurement units. The reference value is an illustrative benchmark, not a verified agronomic target.
For two independent groups, Welch’s t-test allows unequal population variances and is R’s default. Define the contrast order explicitly so the sign of the estimate is unambiguous.

treated <- subset(PlantGrowth, group == "trt2")$weight
welch <- t.test(treated, control, alternative = "two.sided")
welch


    Welch Two Sample t-test

data:  treated and control
t = 2.134, df = 16.786, p-value = 0.0479
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 0.00512787 0.98287213
sample estimates:
mean of x mean of y 
    5.526     5.032 

data.frame(difference_trt2_minus_ctrl = mean(treated) - mean(control),
           lower_95 = welch$conf.int[1], upper_95 = welch$conf.int[2],
           p_value = welch$p.value)

  difference_trt2_minus_ctrl   lower_95  upper_95    p_value
1                      0.494 0.00512787 0.9828721 0.04789926


The t-test assumes independent observations and appropriate conditions for inference on the mean. With small samples, inspect strong skewness and outliers; normality of model errors matters more than the appearance of a pooled distribution. Welch’s test relaxes equal variance, not independence. Do not choose a one-sided alternative after seeing the sign of the difference.

title: 11  Hypothesis tests and confidence intervals
text:
11.5 Paired observations
A paired design compares linked observations, such as before-and-after measurements on the same plots. The analysis uses within-pair differences. It differs from treating the two measurements as unrelated groups.

paired <- read.csv("data/paired_soil.csv")
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(paired$plot_id), complete.cases(paired))
paired$change <- paired$after_mg_kg - paired$before_mg_kg
hist(paired$change, xlab = "Change in available N (mg/kg)", main = "Within-plot changes")







t.test(paired$after_mg_kg, paired$before_mg_kg, paired = TRUE)


    Paired t-test

data:  paired$after_mg_kg and paired$before_mg_kg
t = 6.5908, df = 19, p-value = 2.62e-06
alternative hypothesis: true mean difference is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 3.541818 6.838182
sample estimates:
mean difference 
           5.19 


Pairs must be correctly matched; the differences should be independent across pairs. Normality is assessed for differences, not separately for before and after values. Without an untreated comparison, a before–after increase may reflect time or seasonal effects as well as management.
crumbs: 11  Hypothesis tests and confidence intervals

title: 11  Hypothesis tests and confidence intervals
text:
11.6 Chi-square tests for pest observations
A contingency table cross-classifies counts. In the simulated pest dataset, each independently treated plot contributes one yes/no infestation status at a specified assessment date. The table is not composed of repeated observations of the same insects.

pest <- read.csv("data/pest.csv")
tab <- with(pest, table(treatment, infested))
tab

         infested
treatment No Yes
  Control 20  40
  IPM     46  14

proportions(tab, margin = 1)

         infested
treatment        No       Yes
  Control 0.3333333 0.6666667
  IPM     0.7666667 0.2333333

chi <- chisq.test(tab, correct = FALSE)
chi$expected

         infested
treatment No Yes
  Control 33  27
  IPM     33  27

chi


    Pearson's Chi-squared test

data:  tab
X-squared = 22.761, df = 1, p-value = 1.835e-06


The null hypothesis is independence between treatment and infestation status. Expected counts are calculated under independence, not taken from observed counts. The chi-square approximation needs adequate expected frequencies and independent units. For sparse 2-by-2 tables, Fisher’s exact test is often suitable; it does not fix dependence or poor sampling.

fisher.test(tab)


    Fisher's Exact Test for Count Data

data:  tab
p-value = 3.183e-06
alternative hypothesis: true odds ratio is not equal to 1
95 percent confidence interval:
 0.06268524 0.36395035
sample estimates:
odds ratio 
 0.1549382 


Report infestation proportions and their contrast, not only a test result. Because this example is simulated, no real pest-control efficacy claim follows. In a clustered field survey, observations from the same field may require a model that accounts for clustering.
crumbs: 11  Hypothesis tests and confidence intervals

title: 11  Hypothesis tests and confidence intervals
text:
11.7 What Welch’s test calculates
Suppose two independent groups have sample means \(\bar{x}_1\) and \(\bar{x}_2\), sample variances \(s_1^2\) and \(s_2^2\), and sizes \(n_1\) and \(n_2\). Under a null difference of zero, Welch’s statistic is
\[t=\frac{\bar{x}_1-\bar{x}_2}{\sqrt{s_1^2/n_1+s_2^2/n_2}}.\]
The numerator is the estimated effect. The denominator is its estimated standard error. A difference can therefore produce a larger absolute t-statistic when within-group variation is lower or sample sizes are larger. This does not make the underlying biological difference larger; it changes its precision relative to noise.

n1 <- length(treated); n2 <- length(control)
v1 <- var(treated); v2 <- var(control)
se_difference <- sqrt(v1 / n1 + v2 / n2)
t_manual <- (mean(treated) - mean(control)) / se_difference
df_welch <- (v1 / n1 + v2 / n2)^2 /
  ((v1 / n1)^2 / (n1 - 1) + (v2 / n2)^2 / (n2 - 1))
c(manual_t = t_manual, R_t = unname(welch$statistic),
  manual_df = df_welch, R_df = unname(welch$parameter))

 manual_t       R_t manual_df      R_df 
  2.13402   2.13402  16.78576  16.78576 


The degrees of freedom need not be an integer. They account approximately for uncertainty in the two variance estimates. In contrast, the pooled-variance t-test assumes a common population variance and estimates it using both groups. Choose the method from the design and assumptions rather than selecting whichever one gives a smaller p-value.
crumbs: 11  Hypothesis tests and confidence intervals

title: 11  Hypothesis tests and confidence intervals
section: 11.8 Reading a contingency table cell by cell
text:
11.8 Reading a contingency table cell by cell
Under independence, a contingency table’s expected count is its row total multiplied by its column total and divided by the grand total. For example, if there are 60 control plots and 50 infested plots among 120 plots overall, independence predicts 60 * 50 / 120 = 25 infested control plots. The observed number need not be 25; the difference contributes to the test statistic.

expected_manual <- outer(rowSums(tab), colSums(tab)) / sum(tab)
expected_manual

        No Yes
Control 33  27
IPM     33  27

cell_contributions <- (tab - expected_manual)^2 / expected_manual
cell_contributions

         infested
treatment       No      Yes
  Control 5.121212 6.259259
  IPM     5.121212 6.259259

c(manual_chisq = sum(cell_contributions), R_chisq = unname(chi$statistic))

manual_chisq      R_chisq 
    22.76094     22.76094 


Squaring prevents positive and negative discrepancies from cancelling. Dividing by the expected count scales discrepancies relative to their expected magnitude. In a two-by-two table the independence test has one degree of freedom. In a general r-by-c table it has (r - 1)(c - 1) degrees of freedom when the usual assumptions apply.
A test of association does not by itself give the direction or size of an efficacy effect. Inspect row proportions and define a contrast such as risk difference or risk ratio. If treatments were randomized to independent plots, the contrast can support a treatment interpretation within the experiment’s scope. If farmers chose their treatments, management and pest risk may already differ before treatment.
crumbs: 11  Hypothesis tests and confidence intervals

title: 11  Hypothesis tests and confidence intervals
text:
11.9 Checking assumptions for t-tests
The t-tests above assume approximately normal observations (or differences, for paired data), and the pooled-variance test also assumes equal variances. Plots come first: a histogram, box plot, or normal quantile plot shows the shape of the data. Formal tests can supplement them.

qqnorm(paired$change, main = "Paired differences")
qqline(paired$change)







shapiro.test(paired$change)


    Shapiro-Wilk normality test

data:  paired$change
W = 0.97114, p-value = 0.7788

var.test(treated, control)


    F test to compare two variances

data:  treated and control
F = 0.5761, num df = 9, denom df = 9, p-value = 0.4239
alternative hypothesis: true ratio of variances is not equal to 1
95 percent confidence interval:
 0.1430949 2.3193713
sample estimates:
ratio of variances 
          0.576099 


shapiro.test() tests the null hypothesis that the data come from a normal distribution. var.test() is the F-test for equality of two variances; its statistic is the ratio of the first sample variance to the second. Interpret both with care. With small samples, these tests have little power, so a non-significant result does not prove normality or equal variances. With large samples, they detect departures too small to matter. The t-test is fairly robust to moderate non-normality when the groups are of similar size. Use the tests as one piece of evidence, together with the plots and knowledge of how the data arise; counts and percentages, for example, are rarely normal.
crumbs: 11  Hypothesis tests and confidence intervals

title: 11  Hypothesis tests and confidence intervals
text:
11.10 Tests for proportions
Many agricultural outcomes are proportions: germination, infestation, survival, or adoption of a practice. For a sample of \(n\) independent units of which \(x\) show the outcome, prop.test() tests a hypothesized proportion and gives a confidence interval, and binom.test() gives the exact binomial version.
Suppose 400 seeds are drawn from a seed lot and 332 germinate. Is the germination rate consistent with a stated standard of 80%?

prop.test(x = 332, n = 400, p = 0.80)


    1-sample proportions test with continuity correction

data:  332 out of 400, null probability 0.8
X-squared = 2.0664, df = 1, p-value = 0.1506
alternative hypothesis: true p is not equal to 0.8
95 percent confidence interval:
 0.7887474 0.8647631
sample estimates:
   p 
0.83 

binom.test(x = 332, n = 400, p = 0.80)


    Exact binomial test

data:  332 and 400
number of successes = 332, number of trials = 400, p-value = 0.1503
alternative hypothesis: true probability of success is not equal to 0.8
95 percent confidence interval:
 0.7895289 0.8655028
sample estimates:
probability of success 
                  0.83 


The sample germination is 83%, and the 95% confidence interval for the lot’s germination rate lies roughly between 79% and 86%. It includes 80%, so the data do not show that the lot differs from the standard. If the decision rule requires evidence that the lot exceeds the standard, that one-sided question must be stated before testing, with alternative = "greater".
prop.test() also compares proportions between groups. For two groups it is equivalent to the chi-square test of the 2 × 2 table, and it reports the two proportions and a confidence interval for their difference.

infested <- tab[, "Yes"]
plots <- rowSums(tab)
prop.test(infested, plots, correct = FALSE)


    2-sample test for equality of proportions without continuity correction

data:  infested out of plots
X-squared = 22.761, df = 1, p-value = 1.835e-06
alternative hypothesis: two.sided
95 percent confidence interval:
 0.2730808 0.5935858
sample estimates:
   prop 1    prop 2 
0.6666667 0.2333333 


These methods assume that the units are independent. Seeds in the same tray or plants in the same plot are not independent of each other: tray or plot effects make the outcomes cluster. When the experimental unit is the tray, analyse tray-level percentages, as in the transformation example of Chapter 13.
crumbs: 11  Hypothesis tests and confidence intervals

title: 11  Hypothesis tests and confidence intervals
section: 11.11 Goodness of fit: testing Mendelian ratios
text:
11.11 Goodness of fit: testing Mendelian ratios
A chi-square goodness-of-fit test compares observed counts in categories with the counts expected under a hypothesized ratio. Genetics provides the classic agricultural example. In his experiments with peas, Gregor Mendel crossed plants differing in seed shape and colour and recorded 315 round yellow, 108 round green, 101 wrinkled yellow, and 32 wrinkled green seeds in the second generation. Independent assortment of two genes predicts a 9:3:3:1 ratio.

seeds <- c(round_yellow = 315, round_green = 108,
           wrinkled_yellow = 101, wrinkled_green = 32)
fit_ratio <- chisq.test(seeds, p = c(9, 3, 3, 1) / 16)
fit_ratio


    Chi-squared test for given probabilities

data:  seeds
X-squared = 0.47002, df = 3, p-value = 0.9254

round(fit_ratio$expected, 1)

   round_yellow     round_green wrinkled_yellow  wrinkled_green 
          312.8           104.2           104.2            34.8 


Expected counts are the total, 556, multiplied by 9/16, 3/16, 3/16, and 1/16. The chi-square statistic is small, about 0.47 on 3 degrees of freedom, and the p-value is large. The data are consistent with a 9:3:3:1 ratio. As always, this does not prove the ratio; it shows that the observed deviations are of the size expected from chance.
For a single gene with complete dominance, an F2 generation should segregate 3:1. Mendel’s stem-length cross gave 787 tall and 277 dwarf plants.

chisq.test(c(tall = 787, dwarf = 277), p = c(3, 1) / 4)


    Chi-squared test for given probabilities

data:  c(tall = 787, dwarf = 277)
X-squared = 0.60652, df = 1, p-value = 0.4361


The degrees of freedom are the number of categories minus one. If any parameters of the expected distribution are estimated from the data, one further degree of freedom is lost for each. The approximation is reliable when every expected count is at least about 5.
crumbs: 11  Hypothesis tests and confidence intervals

title: 11  Hypothesis tests and confidence intervals
text:
11.12 When assumptions fail: rank-based tests
When data are clearly non-normal and a transformation is not appropriate, or when the measurements are ranks or scores, rank-based (non-parametric) tests are an alternative. They replace observations by their ranks and so are less affected by skewness and outliers.



Table 11.1: Rank-based alternatives to common tests










Design
Parametric test
Rank-based alternative




Two independent groups
t.test()
wilcox.test() (Wilcoxon rank-sum / Mann–Whitney)


Paired observations
t.test(paired = TRUE)
wilcox.test(paired = TRUE) (Wilcoxon signed-rank)


Three or more independent groups
one-way ANOVA
kruskal.test() (Kruskal–Wallis)







wilcox.test(treated, control, exact = FALSE)


    Wilcoxon rank sum test with continuity correction

data:  treated and control
W = 75, p-value = 0.06402
alternative hypothesis: true location shift is not equal to 0

wilcox.test(paired$after_mg_kg, paired$before_mg_kg, paired = TRUE, exact = FALSE)


    Wilcoxon signed rank test with continuity correction

data:  paired$after_mg_kg and paired$before_mg_kg
V = 206, p-value = 0.0001752
alternative hypothesis: true location shift is not equal to 0

aphid <- read.csv("data/aphid_counts.csv")
kruskal.test(aphids_per_plant ~ treatment, data = aphid)


    Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test

data:  aphids_per_plant by treatment
Kruskal-Wallis chi-squared = 19.973, df = 4, p-value = 0.0005056


exact = FALSE asks for the normal approximation, which is needed when the data contain tied values. The Kruskal–Wallis test on the aphid counts asks whether the treatments differ in the distribution of counts; it is a useful check on the transformed ANOVA in Chapter 13. Rank tests do not estimate a difference in means, and they still assume independent units. They are not a remedy for poor design.
