title: 11  Hypothesis tests and confidence intervals
section: 11.14 Type I error, Type II error, and power
text:
11.14 Type I error, Type II error, and power
A Type I error rejects a true null hypothesis. The chosen significance level controls its probability under the stated test model. A Type II error fails to reject a false null. Power is the probability of rejecting the null for a specified alternative effect and design. Power is therefore not one fixed characteristic of a test: it depends on the effect size, variability, sample size, and significance level.
When planning a trial, specify the smallest difference that would matter scientifically or economically and use a defensible estimate of variation. A pilot trial can inform that estimate, but its uncertainty should be acknowledged. The following planning calculation asks for the approximate sample size per group needed to detect a difference of 0.5 t/ha when the within-group SD is 0.6 t/ha, using a two-sided two-sample test at level 0.05 and power 0.80.

planning <- power.t.test(delta = .5, sd = .6, sig.level = .05,
                         power = .80, type = "two.sample", alternative = "two.sided")
planning


     Two-sample t test power calculation 

              n = 23.60472
          delta = 0.5
             sd = 0.6
      sig.level = 0.05
          power = 0.8
    alternative = two.sided

NOTE: n is number in *each* group

ceiling(planning$n)

[1] 24


This is a simple equal-size independent-group planning example. Blocking, clustering, repeated measurements, unequal allocation, and expected missingness require additional design considerations. Do not use a planning result to justify treating subsamples as independent units. Also, calculating “observed power” from the same estimated effect and p-value after a test adds little information; report the effect and interval instead.
crumbs: 11  Hypothesis tests and confidence intervals

title: 11  Hypothesis tests and confidence intervals
text:
11.15 Confidence intervals and decisions
A 95% confidence procedure has 95% coverage under repeated sampling when its assumptions hold. A particular computed interval is not a 95% probability statement about a fixed parameter in frequentist inference. Wide intervals indicate that both small and large effects may be compatible with the data. Equivalence requires a prespecified margin and an appropriate equivalence analysis; a nonsignificant t-test is insufficient.
If many outcomes or comparisons are tested, false positives become more likely. Prespecify primary comparisons, distinguish exploratory results, and use an appropriate multiplicity method when needed. The next chapter introduces Tukey comparisons after ANOVA.

Numerical and conceptual questions
Answers are given at the end of the chapter.

A sample of 16 plants has mean height 52 cm and SD 8 cm. Test \(H_0: \mu = 50\) cm.
In an F2, 290 tall and 110 dwarf plants are observed. Test a 3:1 ratio.

Important formulae
One-sample t statistic:
\[
t = \frac{\bar x - \mu_0}{s/\sqrt n}
\tag{11.1}\]
Paired t statistic:
\[
t = \frac{\bar d}{s_d/\sqrt n}
\tag{11.2}\]
Pearson’s chi-square statistic:
\[
\chi^2 = \sum \frac{(O_i - E_i)^2}{E_i}
\tag{11.3}\]


Quick revision

Question → \(H_0\) and \(H_1\) → test → p-value → interpretation with an interval.
Paired design → paired test; independent groups → Welch or pooled test.
Counts in categories → chi-square; small expected counts → Fisher’s exact test.
Non-normal small samples → rank-based tests.
Not significant ≠ no effect.

1. null 2. I 3. power 4. paired 5. variances 6. chi-square 7. rank-sum 8. 0.05

By Equation 11.1, \(t = (52-50)/(8/4) = 1.0\) with 15 df; not significant.
Expected 300 and 100; by Equation 11.3, \(\chi^2 = 100/300 + 100/100 = 1.33\) with 1 df; the fit is good.
By Equation 11.2, \(t = 2.62/(4.72/\sqrt{15}) = 2.15\) with 14 df.

12.1 Learning outcomes
Fit a one-way ANOVA, interpret sums of squares and the F-test, check residual diagnostics, use adjusted pairwise comparisons, and include blocks in a simple agricultural experiment.
crumbs: 12  Comparing treatments with analysis of variance

title: 12  Comparing treatments with analysis of variance
text:
12.2 Why ANOVA?
Comparing three or more means by many unadjusted t-tests increases the chance of false-positive conclusions. One-way analysis of variance begins with a global null hypothesis that all group population means are equal. Its model is
\[Y_{ij}=\mu+\tau_i+\epsilon_{ij},\]
where \(\tau_i\) represents a treatment effect and the errors are assumed independent with mean zero and common variance. Normal errors provide the classical small-sample F reference distribution. The test compares treatment mean square with residual mean square. A large F-statistic means between-group variation is large relative to unexplained within-group variation.
crumbs: 12  Comparing treatments with analysis of variance

title: 12  Comparing treatments with analysis of variance
section: 12.3 Worked calculation: separating sources of variation
text:
12.3 Worked calculation: separating sources of variation
Suppose three independently randomized groups have yields A = (3, 4, 5), B = (4, 5, 6), and C = (5, 6, 7) t/ha. The group means are 4, 5, and 6 and the grand mean is 5. For equal group size 3, treatment sum of squares is \(3[(4-5)^2+(5-5)^2+(6-5)^2]=6\). Within each group the squared deviations add to 2, giving residual sum of squares 6 across all groups.
There are 3 - 1 = 2 treatment degrees of freedom and 9 - 3 = 6 residual degrees of freedom. Treatment mean square is 6/2 = 3, residual mean square is 6/6 = 1, and the F-statistic is 3.

toy <- data.frame(group = factor(rep(c("A", "B", "C"), each = 3)),
                  yield_t_ha = c(3, 4, 5, 4, 5, 6, 5, 6, 7))
summary(aov(yield_t_ha ~ group, data = toy))

            Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Pr(>F)
group        2      6       3       3  0.125
Residuals    6      6       1               

pf(3, df1 = 2, df2 = 6, lower.tail = FALSE)

[1] 0.125


The p-value is 0.125. The observed means differ, but the data do not reject the global equality hypothesis at the conventional 0.05 level under this model. “Means differ in this sample” and “there is strong evidence of population differences” are distinct statements. Larger, well-designed replication may improve precision; repeating measurements of the same experimental units does not create new independent replication.

title: 12  Comparing treatments with analysis of variance
text:
12.4 Worked example: plant dry weight

data("PlantGrowth", package = "datasets")
fit <- aov(weight ~ group, data = PlantGrowth)
summary(fit)

            Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Pr(>F)  
group        2  3.766  1.8832   4.846 0.0159 *
Residuals   27 10.492  0.3886                 
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

aggregate(weight ~ group, PlantGrowth, mean)

  group weight
1  ctrl  5.032
2  trt1  4.661
3  trt2  5.526


In the ANOVA table, Df gives degrees of freedom, Sum Sq partitions variation, Mean Sq divides sums of squares by degrees of freedom, and Pr(>F) gives the global p-value. Rejecting the global null indicates evidence that at least one mean differs; it does not show that every pair differs.

TukeyHSD(fit)

  Tukey multiple comparisons of means
    95% family-wise confidence level

Fit: aov(formula = weight ~ group, data = PlantGrowth)

$group
            diff        lwr       upr     p adj
trt1-ctrl -0.371 -1.0622161 0.3202161 0.3908711
trt2-ctrl  0.494 -0.1972161 1.1852161 0.1979960
trt2-trt1  0.865  0.1737839 1.5562161 0.0120064


Tukey’s method adjusts simultaneous pairwise comparisons within the specified family. Each row reports a signed difference, interval, and adjusted p-value. Read the group order carefully. Avoid reducing the entire analysis to letter groupings; report means, differences, uncertainty, and design.

title: 12  Comparing treatments with analysis of variance
section: 12.5 Diagnose the errors, not just the raw observations
text:
12.5 Diagnose the errors, not just the raw observations

old <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(fit, which = 1)
plot(fit, which = 2)







par(old)
boxplot(weight ~ group, PlantGrowth, xlab = "Group", ylab = "Dry weight")








Residual-versus-fitted plots reveal unequal spread and patterns; normal quantile plots reveal departures from a normal error distribution. Neither a diagnostic plot nor a formal normality test can establish independence; that comes from the design. Small samples provide little information about distribution tails. A single normality p-value should not act as an automatic gatekeeper.
If variances differ substantially, Welch’s one-way test is an alternative for independent groups:

oneway.test(weight ~ group, data = PlantGrowth, var.equal = FALSE)


    One-way analysis of means (not assuming equal variances)

data:  weight and group
F = 5.181, num df = 2.000, denom df = 17.128, p-value = 0.01739


Welch’s test does not use the ordinary equal-variance ANOVA error term. Do not follow it automatically with classical TukeyHSD(); choose pairwise methods compatible with unequal variances if needed.

title: 12  Comparing treatments with analysis of variance
text:
12.6 Blocking in agricultural experiments
Field fertility may vary across space. A randomized complete block design assigns every treatment once within each block, with randomization within blocks. The additive model includes both treatment and block:
\[Y_{ij}=\mu+\tau_i+\beta_j+\epsilon_{ij}.\]
The supplied simulated rcbd.csv has six blocks and three treatment plots per block. It differs from the larger crop dataset, which also includes variety and replicate plots. Do not analyze that factorial dataset as though it were this simple RCBD.

rcbd <- read.csv("data/rcbd.csv")
rcbd$block <- factor(rcbd$block)
rcbd$treatment <- factor(rcbd$treatment)
with(rcbd, table(block, treatment))

     treatment
block Compost Control Mineral
    1       1       1       1
    2       1       1       1
    3       1       1       1
    4       1       1       1
    5       1       1       1
    6       1       1       1

blocked <- aov(yield_t_ha ~ block + treatment, data = rcbd)
summary(blocked)

            Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value   Pr(>F)    
block        5  2.378  0.4755   11.16 0.000776 ***
treatment    2  1.545  0.7723   18.13 0.000472 ***
Residuals   10  0.426  0.0426                     
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

TukeyHSD(blocked, "treatment")

  Tukey multiple comparisons of means
    95% family-wise confidence level

Fit: aov(formula = yield_t_ha ~ block + treatment, data = rcbd)

$treatment
                      diff        lwr        upr     p adj
Control-Compost -0.5483333 -0.8749921 -0.2216746 0.0025511
Mineral-Compost  0.1266667 -0.1999921  0.4533254 0.5567094
Mineral-Control  0.6750000  0.3483412  1.0016588 0.0005530


Representing block as a factor avoids imposing a linear trend in arbitrary block numbers. With one plot per treatment in each block, a separate treatment-by-block interaction cannot be estimated independently of residual error. The additive model assumes that interaction is negligible for its intended interpretation. Inference beyond the observed blocks and more complex designs may require mixed models.
Ignoring blocks can waste precision and misrepresent the design. Conversely, adding terms without understanding randomization does not create a valid analysis. The default ANOVA sums of squares are sequential; in unbalanced designs, term order and the exact hypothesis require attention. The balanced examples here keep that issue visible without treating advanced factorial analysis as a one-line extension.

title: 12  Comparing treatments with analysis of variance
section: 12.7 Reading treatment comparisons in their experimental context
text:
12.7 Reading treatment comparisons in their experimental context
Let us distinguish three quantities that are often placed in the same results table: a treatment mean, the standard deviation of individual plots in that treatment, and the standard error of an estimated treatment contrast. The mean describes a central response. The SD describes plot variation. The contrast’s standard error depends on the model and design, including the number of replicates and any blocking adjustment.
For a balanced independent one-way design with r plots per treatment and residual mean square MSE, the standard error of a difference between two treatment means is \(\sqrt{2\,MSE/r}\). In a balanced additive RCBD the analogous contrast uses the residual variance after accounting for blocks. This is why treatment comparisons should use the appropriate model’s error term rather than the spread of the three treatment means.

anova_table <- anova(blocked)
residual_mse <- anova_table["Residuals", "Mean Sq"]
r <- length(unique(rcbd$block))
c(residual_mse = residual_mse,
  standard_error_difference = sqrt(2 * residual_mse / r))

             residual_mse standard_error_difference 
               0.04259889                0.11916220 


This standard error does not itself adjust for examining all treatment pairs. Multiplicity adjustments change the critical comparison or interval construction. A planned comparison identified before data collection may ask a more focused question than all pairwise comparisons, such as average response under two management treatments versus the control. Its weights and intended hypothesis should be stated explicitly.
crumbs: 12  Comparing treatments with analysis of variance

title: 12  Comparing treatments with analysis of variance
section: 12.8 A factorial extension: treatment and variety
text:
12.8 A factorial extension: treatment and variety
In agricultural research, two factors may be applied together. A factorial experiment observes combinations of their levels. Here the larger simulated crop dataset contains three management treatments and two varieties in each of five blocks, with two independently measured plot replicates for each combination. This allows us to illustrate a treatment-by-variety interaction.

crop <- read.csv("data/crop_trial.csv")
crop$block <- factor(crop$block)
crop$treatment <- factor(crop$treatment)
crop$variety <- factor(crop$variety)
with(crop, interaction.plot(treatment, variety, yield_t_ha,
                            xlab = "Management treatment", ylab = "Mean yield (t/ha)",
                            trace.label = "Variety", type = "b", pch = c(16, 17)))







factorial_fit <- aov(yield_t_ha ~ block + treatment * variety, data = crop)
summary(factorial_fit)

                  Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value   Pr(>F)    
block              4  2.286   0.572   4.425  0.00386 ** 
treatment          2 15.291   7.645  59.195 6.55e-14 ***
variety            1  0.821   0.821   6.359  0.01491 *  
treatment:variety  2  0.274   0.137   1.060  0.35398    
Residuals         50  6.458   0.129                     
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


The expression treatment * variety expands to both main effects and their interaction. An interaction means that the difference between varieties depends on management treatment, or equivalently that a management contrast depends on variety. A single overall treatment difference can then conceal an important pattern. Nonparallel sample lines suggest an interaction to examine, but sampling variation can also make them nonparallel.
If interaction is important scientifically, report comparisons within relevant levels with an appropriate simultaneous procedure. Do not interpret a nonsignificant interaction as proof that responses are identical across varieties. Likewise, do not remove an interaction solely to make a main effect significant. Consider the question, precision, and experimental design.
The factorial example assumes both factors were randomized at the plot level within blocks. If irrigation is applied to whole field sections and variety to smaller subplots, the error structure changes. A split-plot experiment needs a split-plot analysis; entering the same factor names into an ordinary one-error ANOVA is not sufficient. Chapter 13 analyses CRD, RCBD, Latin square, factorial, and split-plot experiments in full, including SEm, CD, and CV.
crumbs: 12  Comparing treatments with analysis of variance

title: 12  Comparing treatments with analysis of variance
text:
12.9 Reporting an ANOVA analysis
A useful report identifies the design, factor levels, independent replication, model, and any exclusions before presenting the table. Report treatment estimates with units, the global test and relevant degrees of freedom, the method used for comparisons, and the main diagnostic findings. An agronomic interpretation should explain the size of a response, not merely its statistical label.
For example, a small positive difference with a wide interval may justify a larger experiment rather than a recommendation. A precisely estimated increase may still be uneconomic if the treatment is costly. A trial at one site and season does not establish performance under all environments. These are not flaws that another p-value can repair; they define the scope of the evidence.

title: 13  Designing and analysing field experiments
text:
13.1 Learning outcomes
Explain replication, randomization, and local control; randomize CRD, RCBD, and Latin square layouts in R; analyse completely randomized, randomized block, Latin square, two-factor factorial, and split-plot experiments; calculate and interpret SEm, SEd, critical difference (CD), and coefficient of variation (CV); transform counts and percentages when their variance depends on the mean; and choose a mean-comparison procedure that matches the question.
The previous chapter introduced analysis of variance with one treatment factor. This chapter turns to the experiments that agricultural students actually lay out in pots, nurseries, and fields. The emphasis is on one rule that runs through every design: the analysis must follow the way treatments were randomized to experimental units.
crumbs: 13  Designing and analysing field experiments

title: 13  Designing and analysing field experiments
text:
13.2 Three principles of experimental design
R. A. Fisher’s work at Rothamsted gave agricultural research three principles that remain the foundation of every field trial.
Replication. Each treatment is applied to more than one experimental unit. Replication lets us estimate experimental error, the variation between units treated alike. Without it, a difference between two plots cannot be separated from ordinary plot-to-plot variation. More replicates also make treatment means more precise.
Randomization. Treatments are allocated to units by a chance mechanism, not by the researcher’s choice. Randomization protects comparisons from systematic bias, such as always placing the favoured treatment on the best soil, and it justifies the error estimate used in the F-test.
Local control. Units are grouped so that variation within groups is small. Blocks across a fertility gradient, rows and columns in a field with two gradients, and main plots for hard-to-change factors are all forms of local control. Grouping removes known variation from the error term and increases precision.






Identify the experimental unit first



The experimental unit is the smallest unit to which a treatment is independently applied: a pot, a plot, a tree, a tray. Five plants sampled from one plot are subsamples, not five replicates. If irrigation is applied to whole strips, the strip is the unit for irrigation even when nitrogen is varied within it. Every design in this chapter is a statement about experimental units.


A few terms recur. A treatment is a condition being compared (a variety, a fertilizer dose, a spray schedule). A factor is a set of related treatments, and its levels are the individual treatments. The response is the measurement on each unit, here usually grain yield or dry matter. Experimental error is the variation among units that received the same treatment.
crumbs: 13  Designing and analysing field experiments

title: 13  Designing and analysing field experiments
text:
13.3 Randomizing a layout in R
Randomization should be done before the experiment and recorded. sample() returns a random permutation; set.seed() makes the permutation reproducible, so the layout can be regenerated and checked later. Use a new seed for each real experiment and keep it with the field book.

13.3.1 Completely randomized layout
In a completely randomized design (CRD), every unit has the same chance of receiving any treatment. With five treatments and four replicates there are 20 units, and we randomly permute 20 treatment labels.

set.seed(2026)
treatments <- c("N0", "N40", "N80", "N120", "N160")
crd_plan <- data.frame(pot = 1:20,
                       treatment = sample(rep(treatments, times = 4)))
head(crd_plan, 8)

  pot treatment
1   1        N0
2   2        N0
3   3       N80
4   4      N160
5   5        N0
6   6       N40
7   7      N120
8   8      N160

table(crd_plan$treatment)


  N0 N120 N160  N40  N80 
   4    4    4    4    4 


The table() check confirms that every treatment appears exactly four times. Write the pot numbers on labels before allocating treatments, so that the random plan, not convenience, decides which pot receives which dose.


13.3.2 Randomized complete block layout
In a randomized complete block design (RCBD), every treatment appears once in each block, and randomization is carried out separately within each block.

set.seed(2026)
varieties <- paste0("V", 1:6)
blocks <- 4
rcbd_plan <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:blocks, function(b)
  data.frame(block = b, plot_in_block = 1:6, variety = sample(varieties))))
head(rcbd_plan, 6)

  block plot_in_block variety
1     1             1      V5
2     1             2      V1
3     1             3      V6
4     1             4      V2
5     1             5      V4
6     1             6      V3

# Field plan: one row per block, plots in field order
matrix(rcbd_plan$variety, nrow = blocks, byrow = TRUE,
       dimnames = list(paste("Block", 1:blocks), paste("Plot", 1:6)))

        Plot 1 Plot 2 Plot 3 Plot 4 Plot 5 Plot 6
Block 1 "V5"   "V1"   "V6"   "V2"   "V4"   "V3"  
Block 2 "V3"   "V4"   "V5"   "V1"   "V6"   "V2"  
Block 3 "V2"   "V6"   "V4"   "V3"   "V1"   "V5"  
Block 4 "V6"   "V1"   "V4"   "V2"   "V3"   "V5"  


Each row of the field plan is a block and contains all six varieties in a different random order. Blocks should be laid out across the known gradient, so that plots within a block are as similar as possible.


13.3.3 Latin square layout
A Latin square controls variation in two directions. With five treatments, the field is divided into five rows and five columns, and each treatment appears once in every row and once in every column. A simple way to obtain a random Latin square is to start from a cyclic square and then randomly permute its rows, columns, and treatment labels.

set.seed(2026)
k <- 5
cyclic <- outer(0:(k - 1), 0:(k - 1), function(i, j) (i + j) %% k) + 1
square <- cyclic[sample(k), sample(k)]
labels <- sample(c("A", "B", "C", "D", "E"))
ls_plan <- matrix(labels[square], nrow = k,
                  dimnames = list(paste("Row", 1:k), paste("Col", 1:k)))
ls_plan

      Col 1 Col 2 Col 3 Col 4 Col 5
Row 1 "E"   "C"   "D"   "A"   "B"  
Row 2 "C"   "A"   "B"   "D"   "E"  
Row 3 "B"   "E"   "A"   "C"   "D"  
Row 4 "A"   "D"   "E"   "B"   "C"  
Row 5 "D"   "B"   "C"   "E"   "A"  

# Every treatment once per row and once per column
all(apply(ls_plan, 1, function(x) length(unique(x)) == k),
    apply(ls_plan, 2, function(x) length(unique(x)) == k))

[1] TRUE




13.3.4 Layouts with the agricolae package
The agricolae package, widely used in agricultural statistics teaching, creates field books for many designs. Its book component lists plots, blocks, and treatments ready for printing.

library(agricolae)
crd_book <- design.crd(trt = treatments, r = 4, seed = 2026, serie = 0)
head(crd_book$book)

  plots r treatments
1     1 1        N80
2     2 2        N80
3     3 1         N0
4     4 1        N40
5     5 1       N120
6     6 1       N160

rcbd_book <- design.rcbd(trt = varieties, r = 4, seed = 2026, serie = 2)
head(rcbd_book$book)

  plots block varieties
1   101     1        V1
2   102     1        V2
3   103     1        V4
4   104     1        V6
5   105     1        V3
6   106     1        V5


Whichever tool you use, store the seed, the software version, and the printed plan. A layout that cannot be reproduced cannot be audited.

title: 13  Designing and analysing field experiments
section: 13.4 Quantities reported with every field experiment
text:
13.4 Quantities reported with every field experiment
Agricultural research reports in India conventionally present, below each table of treatment means, the standard error of a mean, the critical difference, and the coefficient of variation. They all come from the error mean square (MSE) of the analysis.



Table 13.1: Standard summary quantities for a single-factor design










Quantity
Formula
Meaning




SEm±
\(\sqrt{MSE/r}\)
Standard error of one treatment mean based on \(r\) replicates


SEd
\(\sqrt{2\,MSE/r}\)
Standard error of the difference between two treatment means


CD (5%)
\(t_{0.025,\ \text{error df}} \times \text{SEd}\)
Least difference between two means that is significant at 5%


CV (%)
\(100\sqrt{MSE}/\bar{y}\)
Experimental error relative to the general mean






The CV describes the precision of the experiment as a whole. Typical values depend on the crop, the character, and the conditions; yield trials commonly have smaller CVs than pest counts or weed biomass. A very high CV signals poor control of experimental error, and a very low CV in a field trial is worth double-checking for data-entry problems.
The CD is the classical least significant difference (LSD). Two treatment means that differ by more than the CD differ significantly at the 5% level, provided the F-test for treatments was significant and the comparison was of interest before the data were seen. We return to this condition in Section 13.11.
We will compute these quantities often, so we write one small function. It works for any aov() fit without an Error() term, given the number of replicates behind each mean.

design_stats <- function(fit, r, alpha = 0.05) {
  mse <- deviance(fit) / df.residual(fit)
  sem <- sqrt(mse / r)
  sed <- sqrt(2 * mse / r)
  cd <- qt(1 - alpha / 2, df = df.residual(fit)) * sed
  response <- fitted(fit) + residuals(fit)
  cv <- 100 * sqrt(mse) / mean(response)
  round(c(MSE = mse, SEm = sem, SEd = sed, CD = cd, CV_percent = cv), 3)
}

deviance() of an aov fit is the residual sum of squares, and df.residual() gives its degrees of freedom. Adding the fitted values and residuals recovers the observed response, so the CV uses the general mean of the data.
crumbs: 13  Designing and analysing field experiments

title: 13  Designing and analysing field experiments
text:
13.5 Completely randomized design
A CRD is appropriate when the experimental units are homogeneous, for example pots filled from one thoroughly mixed soil, petri dishes in an incubator, or uniform nursery trays. It is rarely suitable for open field trials, where soil fertility varies from place to place.
The model is the one-way model from the previous chapter, \(Y_{ij} = \mu + \tau_i + \epsilon_{ij}\). The simulated file crd.csv records dry matter (g per pot) in a pot experiment with five nitrogen levels and four pots per level.

crd <- read.csv("data/crd.csv")
crd$nitrogen <- factor(crd$nitrogen,
                       levels = c("N0", "N40", "N80", "N120", "N160"))
table(crd$nitrogen)


  N0  N40  N80 N120 N160 
   4    4    4    4    4 

crd_fit <- aov(dry_matter_g_pot ~ nitrogen, data = crd)
summary(crd_fit)

            Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value   Pr(>F)    
nitrogen     4  323.4   80.86   16.04 2.71e-05 ***
Residuals   15   75.6    5.04                     
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

crd_means <- tapply(crd$dry_matter_g_pot, crd$nitrogen, mean)
round(crd_means, 2)

   N0   N40   N80  N120  N160 
18.32 23.55 24.42 28.90 29.32 

design_stats(crd_fit, r = 4)

       MSE        SEm        SEd         CD CV_percent 
     5.042      1.123      1.588      3.384      9.016 


Setting the factor levels puts the doses in their natural order; otherwise R sorts labels alphabetically and places N120 before N40. The F-test is highly significant, so there is strong evidence that mean dry matter differs among the nitrogen levels.
The CV is about 9%, and the CD is about 3.4 g per pot. Mean dry matter rose from about 18.3 g at N0 to about 29.3 g at N160. N40 and N80 differ by less than the CD, as do N120 and N160, so the data do not separate those adjacent pairs. Every other comparison with N0 exceeds the CD.
Because nitrogen levels are quantitative, a response curve answers the agronomic question better than a list of pairwise comparisons. A regression of dry matter on dose estimates how fast the response rises and where it levels off (see the regression chapter). Pairwise comparisons of doses are most useful when the levels are qualitative, such as varieties or products.
crumbs: 13  Designing and analysing field experiments

title: 13  Designing and analysing field experiments
text:
13.6 Randomized complete block design
The RCBD is the most widely used design in field experiments. Blocks are formed across the main gradient of soil fertility, slope, or drainage, and each block contains every treatment once. The additive model is \(Y_{ij} = \mu + \tau_i + \beta_j + \epsilon_{ij}\), where \(\beta_j\) is the effect of block \(j\).
The simulated file rcbd_varieties.csv contains grain yields (t/ha) of six rice varieties (generic labels V1 to V6) in four blocks.

rb <- read.csv("data/rcbd_varieties.csv")
rb$block <- factor(rb$block)
rb$variety <- factor(rb$variety)
with(rb, table(variety, block))  # each variety once in each block

       block
variety 1 2 3 4
     V1 1 1 1 1
     V2 1 1 1 1
     V3 1 1 1 1
     V4 1 1 1 1
     V5 1 1 1 1
     V6 1 1 1 1

rb_fit <- aov(yield_t_ha ~ block + variety, data = rb)
summary(rb_fit)

            Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value  Pr(>F)    
block        3 1.5082  0.5027   12.99 0.00019 ***
variety      5 3.0359  0.6072   15.69 1.7e-05 ***
Residuals   15 0.5806  0.0387                    
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

round(sort(tapply(rb$yield_t_ha, rb$variety, mean), decreasing = TRUE), 2)

  V1   V3   V4   V2   V6   V5 
5.66 5.18 5.15 4.99 4.88 4.48 

design_stats(rb_fit, r = 4)

       MSE        SEm        SEd         CD CV_percent 
     0.039      0.098      0.139      0.297      3.890 


The block line of the ANOVA table shows that blocks differed substantially. Including them in the model removed that variation from the error term. The varietal differences are highly significant, the CV is about 3.9%, and the CD is about 0.30 t/ha. V1 gave the highest mean yield, about 5.66 t/ha; its margin over the next variety, V3, is about 0.49 t/ha, which exceeds the CD.

13.6.1 Did blocking help?
We can compare the error mean square from the blocked analysis with the error that a CRD analysis of the same data would have produced. The relative efficiency (RE) of the RCBD compared with a CRD is
\[RE = \frac{(r-1)E_b + r(t-1)E_e}{(rt-1)E_e},\]
where \(E_b\) is the block mean square, \(E_e\) the error mean square, \(r\) the number of blocks, and \(t\) the number of treatments.

tab <- anova(rb_fit)
Eb <- tab["block", "Mean Sq"]
Ee <- tab["Residuals", "Mean Sq"]
r <- nlevels(rb$block); t <- nlevels(rb$variety)
RE <- ((r - 1) * Eb + r * (t - 1) * Ee) / ((r * t - 1) * Ee)
round(RE, 2)

[1] 2.56

# Error mean square if blocks are ignored
anova(aov(yield_t_ha ~ variety, data = rb))["Residuals", "Mean Sq"]

[1] 0.1160444


An RE of about 2.6 means that a CRD would have needed roughly 2.6 times as many replicates to estimate the variety means with the same precision. Ignoring the blocks triples the error mean square, from about 0.039 to 0.116. Blocking was clearly worthwhile in this field. Remember, though, that blocks must be part of the analysis because they were part of the randomization, not because they happened to be useful.
crumbs: 13  Designing and analysing field experiments

title: 13  Designing and analysing field experiments
text:
13.7 Latin square design
When a field has two gradients at right angles, for example a slope in one direction and an irrigation channel along another, a Latin square removes both. Each treatment occurs once in every row and every column, so the number of replicates equals the number of treatments. This restricts the Latin square to about four to eight treatments.
The model is \(Y_{ijk} = \mu + \rho_i + \gamma_j + \tau_k + \epsilon_{ijk}\), with row (\(\rho\)), column (\(\gamma\)), and treatment (\(\tau\)) effects. The simulated file latin_square.csv compares five weed-management treatments in a 5 × 5 square.

ls <- read.csv("data/latin_square.csv")
for (v in c("row", "column", "treatment")) ls[[v]] <- factor(ls[[v]])
# Field plan as recorded
xtabs(~ row + column, data = ls)  # one plot per cell

   column
row 1 2 3 4 5
  1 1 1 1 1 1
  2 1 1 1 1 1
  3 1 1 1 1 1
  4 1 1 1 1 1
  5 1 1 1 1 1

matrix(as.character(ls$treatment), nrow = 5, byrow = TRUE)

     [,1]             [,2]             [,3]             [,4]            
[1,] "Unweeded"       "Mulch"          "Pre-emergence"  "Hand weeding"  
[2,] "Mulch"          "Post-emergence" "Hand weeding"   "Unweeded"      
[3,] "Hand weeding"   "Unweeded"       "Post-emergence" "Pre-emergence" 
[4,] "Pre-emergence"  "Hand weeding"   "Mulch"          "Post-emergence"
[5,] "Post-emergence" "Pre-emergence"  "Unweeded"       "Mulch"         
     [,5]            
[1,] "Post-emergence"
[2,] "Pre-emergence" 
[3,] "Mulch"         
[4,] "Unweeded"      
[5,] "Hand weeding"  

ls_fit <- aov(yield_t_ha ~ row + column + treatment, data = ls)
summary(ls_fit)

            Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value   Pr(>F)    
row          4  1.443  0.3607   24.46 1.08e-05 ***
column       4  1.396  0.3489   23.65 1.29e-05 ***
treatment    4  6.708  1.6770  113.70 1.98e-09 ***
Residuals   12  0.177  0.0147                     
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

round(sort(tapply(ls$yield_t_ha, ls$treatment, mean), decreasing = TRUE), 2)

  Hand weeding Post-emergence  Pre-emergence          Mulch       Unweeded 
          4.47           4.11           4.03           3.78           2.93 

design_stats(ls_fit, r = 5)

       MSE        SEm        SEd         CD CV_percent 
     0.015      0.054      0.077      0.167      3.144 


Both rows and columns account for significant variation, which confirms that the field had two gradients. Hand weeding gave the highest mean yield and the unweeded check the lowest. The error has \((t-1)(t-2) = 12\) degrees of freedom. With small squares, such as 4 × 4, the error degrees of freedom become few; the experiment may then be repeated as several squares.
crumbs: 13  Designing and analysing field experiments

title: 13  Designing and analysing field experiments
text:
13.8 Factorial experiments
Often we want to study two or more factors together: nitrogen dose with variety, or irrigation with mulching. In a factorial experiment, every combination of the factor levels is a treatment. A 3 × 2 factorial of three nitrogen levels and two varieties has six treatment combinations, and these are laid out like ordinary treatments, here in an RCBD.
A factorial experiment answers three questions at once:

Main effect of nitrogen: how does yield change with dose, averaged over varieties?
Main effect of variety: how do varieties differ, averaged over doses?
Interaction: does the response to nitrogen depend on the variety?


fa <- read.csv("data/factorial_rcbd.csv")
fa$block <- factor(fa$block)
fa$nitrogen <- factor(fa$nitrogen, levels = c("N0", "N60", "N120"))
fa$variety <- factor(fa$variety)
fa_fit <- aov(yield_t_ha ~ block + nitrogen * variety, data = fa)
summary(fa_fit)

                 Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value   Pr(>F)    
block             3  0.543   0.181   3.499  0.04197 *  
nitrogen          2 10.012   5.006  96.712 2.68e-09 ***
variety           1  2.561   2.561  49.478 4.04e-06 ***
nitrogen:variety  2  0.776   0.388   7.496  0.00553 ** 
Residuals        15  0.776   0.052                     
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

# Two-way table of means
round(with(fa, tapply(yield_t_ha, list(nitrogen, variety), mean)), 2)

     Dwarf Tall
N0    3.24 3.02
N60   4.49 3.86
N120  5.24 4.13


nitrogen * variety expands to nitrogen + variety + nitrogen:variety. The interaction is significant, so the main effects should not be interpreted on their own.

with(fa, interaction.plot(nitrogen, variety, yield_t_ha, type = "b",
                          pch = c(16, 17), xlab = "Nitrogen level",
                          ylab = "Mean yield (t/ha)", trace.label = "Variety"))








The table and plot show the pattern. At N0 the two varieties yield almost the same, but the dwarf variety responds much more strongly to nitrogen: at N120 it out-yields the tall variety by about 1.1 t/ha. The tall variety gains little beyond N60. An agronomic recommendation therefore depends on variety, and an “average response to nitrogen” would describe neither variety well.

13.8.1 Standard errors in a factorial experiment
Means of different kinds rest on different numbers of plots, so each has its own SEd. With \(r\) blocks, \(a\) levels of nitrogen, and \(b\) levels of variety:



Table 13.2: SEd for the different means of a two-factor experiment





Comparison
SEd




Two nitrogen means (averaged over varieties)
\(\sqrt{2\,MSE/(rb)}\)


Two variety means (averaged over nitrogen)
\(\sqrt{2\,MSE/(ra)}\)


Two treatment-combination means
\(\sqrt{2\,MSE/r}\)







mse <- deviance(fa_fit) / df.residual(fa_fit)
r <- 4; a <- 3; b <- 2
sed <- c(nitrogen = sqrt(2 * mse / (r * b)),
         variety = sqrt(2 * mse / (r * a)),
         combination = sqrt(2 * mse / r))
cd <- qt(0.975, df.residual(fa_fit)) * sed
round(rbind(SEd = sed, CD = cd), 3)

    nitrogen variety combination
SEd    0.114   0.093       0.161
CD     0.242   0.198       0.343


When the interaction is significant, compare nitrogen levels within each variety, using the combination CD. For example, the dwarf variety’s gain from N60 to N120 is about 0.75 t/ha, well above the combination CD of about 0.34 t/ha, whereas the tall variety’s gain is only about 0.28 t/ha, below it.
crumbs: 13  Designing and analysing field experiments

title: 13  Designing and analysing field experiments
text:
13.9 Split-plot design
Some factors are impractical to apply to small plots. Irrigation, tillage, and sowing date need large areas, whereas varieties or nitrogen doses can be applied to small plots. In a split-plot design, each block is divided into main plots that receive the levels of the hard-to-change factor, and each main plot is divided into subplots that receive the levels of the second factor. There are two randomizations: main-plot treatments to main plots within each block, then subplot treatments to subplots within each main plot.
Because of the two randomizations there are two error terms:

Error (a), variation among main plots treated alike, is used to test the main-plot factor. It usually has few degrees of freedom and is larger.
Error (b), variation among subplots within main plots, is used to test the subplot factor and the interaction. It is usually smaller, so subplot comparisons are more precise.

The simulated file split_plot.csv contains three irrigation schedules (main plots) and four nitrogen levels (subplots) in three blocks.

sp <- read.csv("data/split_plot.csv")
sp$block <- factor(sp$block)
sp$irrigation <- factor(sp$irrigation)
sp$nitrogen <- factor(sp$nitrogen, levels = c("N0", "N50", "N100", "N150"))
sp_fit <- aov(yield_t_ha ~ irrigation * nitrogen + Error(block / irrigation),
              data = sp)
summary(sp_fit)


Error: block
          Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Pr(>F)
Residuals  2  4.204   2.102               

Error: block:irrigation
           Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Pr(>F)  
irrigation  2 10.686   5.343   17.98   0.01 *
Residuals   4  1.188   0.297                 
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Error: Within
                    Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value   Pr(>F)    
nitrogen             3 13.695   4.565 226.471 1.77e-14 ***
irrigation:nitrogen  6  0.587   0.098   4.851  0.00412 ** 
Residuals           18  0.363   0.020                     
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

round(with(sp, tapply(yield_t_ha, list(irrigation, nitrogen), mean)), 2)

     N0  N50 N100 N150
I1 3.07 4.06 4.42 4.37
I2 4.07 4.90 5.27 5.55
I3 4.07 5.18 5.66 6.13


Error(block / irrigation) tells R that main plots are identified by block and irrigation together. R then splits the analysis into strata. In the block:irrigation stratum, irrigation is tested against error (a), which has only 4 degrees of freedom. In the Within stratum, nitrogen and the interaction are tested against error (b).

13.9.1 What goes wrong if the design is ignored
It is tempting to analyse the same data as an ordinary RCBD with nine treatment combinations.

wrong_fit <- aov(yield_t_ha ~ block + irrigation * nitrogen, data = sp)
summary(wrong_fit)

                    Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value   Pr(>F)    
block                2  4.204   2.102  29.811 5.45e-07 ***
irrigation           2 10.686   5.343  75.779 1.36e-10 ***
nitrogen             3 13.695   4.565  64.745 4.45e-11 ***
irrigation:nitrogen  6  0.587   0.098   1.387    0.264    
Residuals           22  1.551   0.071                     
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


The two analyses disagree sharply. The wrong analysis tests irrigation against a pooled error that mixes main-plot and subplot variation, which inflates its F-value from about 18 to about 76. At the same time, it pools the larger main-plot variation into the error for nitrogen and the interaction. The interaction, highly significant in the correct analysis, is not significant in the wrong one. Same data, same R function, different conclusions: only the analysis that follows the randomization is valid.
The correct analysis shows that the response to nitrogen depends on irrigation. Under the least irrigation (I1), yield levels off after N100, whereas under I3 it is still rising at N150. This is exactly the kind of finding a split-plot experiment is designed to reveal.
The agricolae function sp.plot() produces the same split-plot ANOVA in the traditional layout with error (a) and error (b), which is a useful cross-check.

with(sp, sp.plot(block, irrigation, nitrogen, yield_t_ha))


ANALYSIS SPLIT PLOT:  yield_t_ha 
Class level information

irrigation  :  I3 I2 I1 
nitrogen    :  N100 N0 N50 N150 
block   :  1 2 3 

Number of observations:  36 

Analysis of Variance Table

Response: yield_t_ha
                    Df  Sum Sq Mean Sq  F value    Pr(>F)    
block                2  4.2038  2.1019 104.2749 1.262e-10 ***
irrigation           2 10.6860  5.3430  17.9848  0.010015 *  
Ea                   4  1.1883  0.2971                       
nitrogen             3 13.6952  4.5651 226.4713 1.776e-14 ***
irrigation:nitrogen  6  0.5867  0.0978   4.8509  0.004124 ** 
Eb                  18  0.3628  0.0202                       
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

cv(a) = 11.5 %, cv(b) = 3 %, Mean = 4.731111 


Comparisons in a split-plot need care, because different comparisons use different errors. Two main-plot means use error (a); two subplot means at the same main-plot level use error (b); two subplot means at different main-plot levels combine both errors. Standard textbooks such as Gomez and Gomez (1984) give these formulas. In practice, state which comparison you are making and which error it uses.
crumbs: 13  Designing and analysing field experiments

title: 13  Designing and analysing field experiments
text:
13.10 Checking assumptions and transforming data
The F-test assumes that errors are independent, have constant variance, and are approximately normal. Independence comes from randomization. Constant variance and normality are checked with the residuals of the fitted model, as in the previous chapter.

old <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(rb_fit, which = 1)
plot(rb_fit, which = 2)







par(old)

Agricultural data often break the constant-variance assumption in a predictable way. Counts, such as insects per plant or weeds per quadrat, have variance that increases with the mean. Percentages based on counts, such as germination or disease incidence, have small variance near 0% and 100% and large variance near 50%. For such data a transformation can stabilize the variance before analysis.

13.10.1 Counts: square-root transformation
The simulated file aphid_counts.csv records aphids per plant under five treatments in a CRD with five plants each.

ap <- read.csv("data/aphid_counts.csv")
ap$treatment <- factor(ap$treatment)
# Mean and variance by treatment: variance rises with the mean

13.10.2 Percentages: angular (arcsine) transformation
For percentages from counts, the angular transformation \(\sin^{-1}\sqrt{p}\) stabilizes the variance, where \(p\) is the proportion. It is most useful when many values lie below 30% or above 70%.

ge$seed_treatment <- factor(ge$seed_treatment)
ge$angle_deg <- asin(sqrt(ge$germination_pct / 100)) * 180 / pi
ge_fit <- aov(angle_deg ~ seed_treatment, data = ge)
summary(ge_fit)

               Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value   Pr(>F)    
seed_treatment  3 1448.1   482.7   40.88 1.41e-06 ***
Residuals      12  141.7    11.8

data.frame(mean_pct = tapply(ge$germination_pct, ge$seed_treatment, mean),

           back_transformed_pct = round(100 * sin(angle_means * pi / 180)^2, 1))

Hot water     72.5      58.42                 72.6
KNO3          84.0      66.53                 84.1
Untreated     56.5      48.77                 56.6


asin() returns radians; multiplying by 180 / pi gives degrees, the scale used in most agricultural tables.






Transformations and modern alternatives



Transformations are the classical remedy and remain common in Indian agricultural research reports. Generalized linear models, such as Poisson models for counts and binomial models for germination, analyse the data on their original scale. They are beyond this introductory course but worth knowing about when you meet them in journals. A transformation should be chosen because of the type of data, not because it makes a result significant.

13.11 Comparing treatment means
A significant F-test says that at least one treatment mean differs. Researchers then want to know which ones. Several procedures are in common use, and they answer slightly different questions.



Table 13.3: Common procedures for comparing treatment means










Procedure
What it controls
When it is suitable




CD / LSD
Error rate of each comparison
Planned comparisons, or a few comparisons after a significant F-test (Fisher’s protected LSD)


Duncan’s multiple range test (DMRT)
Error rate that depends on how far apart means are in the ranking
Traditionally used to rank many varieties; widely seen in Indian journals


Tukey’s HSD
Error rate for the whole family of pairwise comparisons
All pairwise comparisons, when false positives are costly

title: 13  Designing and analysing field experiments
text:
13.12 Missing plots and other designs
Plots are sometimes lost to flooding, animals, or theft. In a balanced design, a missing plot makes the data unbalanced. Classical textbooks give formulas to estimate a single missing value in an RCBD or Latin square. Software that fits the model by least squares, including lm(), can analyse unbalanced data directly, but with unbalanced data the order of terms in aov() matters, and the interpretation needs more care. Record why each plot is missing; if losses depend on the treatment, they are themselves a result.
Other designs are used in agricultural research for special situations: augmented designs for screening many germplasm lines with limited seed, lattice and alpha designs for large variety trials where complete blocks would be too big, and strip-plot designs where two factors are both applied to strips. They follow the same principles but need a dedicated text, such as Gomez and Gomez’s Statistical Procedures for Agricultural Research.
crumbs: 13  Designing and analysing field experiments

title: 13  Designing and analysing field experiments
text:
13.13 Reporting a field experiment
A complete report of a designed experiment states:

The design, number of treatments, replications, and plot size, and how randomization was done.
The experimental unit and any subsampling.
A table of treatment means with units, followed by SEm±, CD (5%), and CV (%).
The F-test results and the mean-comparison procedure used.
Any transformation, missing plots, and diagnostic findings.
An agronomic interpretation of the size of the differences, not only their significance.


report <- data.frame(Variety = names(sort(tapply(rb$yield_t_ha, rb$variety, mean),
                                          decreasing = TRUE)),
                     Yield_t_ha = round(sort(tapply(rb$yield_t_ha, rb$variety, mean),
                                             decreasing = TRUE), 2),
                     row.names = NULL)
stats <- design_stats(rb_fit, r = 4)
report

  Variety Yield_t_ha
1      V1       5.66
2      V3       5.18
3      V4       5.15
4      V2       4.99
5      V6       4.88
6      V5       4.48

cat(sprintf("SEm± = %.3f t/ha; CD (5%%) = %.2f t/ha; CV = %.1f%%\n",
            stats["SEm"], stats["CD"], stats["CV_percent"]))

SEm± = 0.098 t/ha; CD (5%) = 0.30 t/ha; CV = 3.9%


A suitable sentence would read: “Varieties differed significantly in grain yield (RCBD, four replications; F = 15.7 on 5 and 15 df, p < 0.001). V1 gave the highest yield (5.66 t/ha), exceeding the next best variety by 0.49 t/ha, more than the CD of 0.30 t/ha.” The numbers come from the analysis, and the chapter on reproducible reports shows how to insert them automatically.

Generate and print a randomized field plan for an RCBD with seven treatments and three blocks. Record the seed.

title: 13  Designing and analysing field experiments
text:
13.15 Live R laboratory

Analyse a randomized block experiment
Edit the code, then select Run R. The first run downloads R into your browser and may take a little time. Copy code also lets you use this example in RStudio.
yield <- c(4.8, 5.4, 4.0, 5.5,
           4.6, 4.9, 4.1, 5.3,
           4.1, 5.0, 3.5, 5.1)
trial <- data.frame(
  block = factor(rep(1:3, each = 4)),
  variety = factor(rep(c("V1", "V2", "V3", "V4"), times = 3)),
  yield = yield)
fit <- aov(yield ~ block + variety, data = trial)
summary(fit)
mse <- deviance(fit) / df.residual(fit)
r <- 3
c(SEm = sqrt(mse / r),
  CD_5pc = qt(0.975, df.residual(fit)) * sqrt(2 * mse / r),
  CV_pc = 100 * sqrt(mse) / mean(yield))
tapply(trial$yield, trial$variety, mean)
Investigate. Remove block + from the model and rerun. How do the error mean square and CD change? Explain why the blocked model is the correct one for this design.







From the browser to your practical notebook



Record the input you changed, the output you obtained, and your interpretation. These live examples use base R and work independently. The full chapter examples, including package-based analyses, remain available with copy buttons for RStudio. Browser objects last until this page is reloaded; Reset code restores the editor text. Internet access is needed on first use; long or interactive desktop tasks belong in RStudio.








Historical Insights



R. A. Fisher set out the principles of replication, randomisation and local control in The Design of Experiments (1935). Latin squares were studied by the mathematician Leonhard Euler in the eighteenth century, long before their use in field trials.








Quotes to Inspire



“To consult the statistician after an experiment is finished is often merely to ask him to conduct a post mortem examination. He can perhaps say what the experiment died of.”
R. A. Fisher, Presidential Address to the First Indian Statistical Congress (1938)

title: 13  Designing and analysing field experiments
text:
13.16 Chapter Summary

Fill in the blanks
Answers are given at the end of the chapter.

The three basic principles of experimental design are replication, randomisation and local __________.
In a CRD, treatments are allocated to all units completely at __________.
An RCBD with \(t\) treatments and \(r\) blocks has __________ error degrees of freedom.
A Latin square controls variation in __________ directions.
In a split-plot design the main-plot factor is tested against error __________.
The __________ is the smallest difference between two means that is significant.
Counts are usually transformed by the __________ transformation.
Percentages are usually transformed by the __________ transformation.



Short-answer questions

Explain the three principles of experimental design.
When is an RCBD preferred to a CRD?
Why does a split-plot design have two error terms?
Define SEm, SEd, CD and CV.
How is the efficiency of blocking measured?



Numerical and conceptual questions
Answers are given at the end of the chapter.

An RCBD has 6 treatments in 4 blocks. Find the error df.
A 5 × 5 Latin square is used. Find the error df.
An RCBD has MSE = 2.5 with \(r = 4\) and 15 error df (\(t_{0.025,15} = 2.131\)). Find SEd and CD.
A split-plot has 4 replications, 3 main plots and 5 sub-plots. Find the df of errors (a) and (b).



Important formulae
Coefficient of variation of an experiment:
\[
\text{CV} = \frac{\sqrt{\text{MSE}}}{\bar y} \times 100
\tag{13.1}\]
Standard error of a mean and of a difference:
\[
\text{SE}(m) = \sqrt{\frac{\text{MSE}}{r}}, \qquad \text{SE}(d) = \sqrt{\frac{2\,\text{MSE}}{r}}
\tag{13.2}\]
Critical difference:
\[
\text{CD} = t_{\alpha/2,\,\text{edf}} \times \text{SE}(d)
\tag{13.3}\]
Relative efficiency of RCBD over CRD:
\[
\text{RE} = \frac{(r-1)E_b + r(t-1)E_e}{(rt-1)E_e}
\tag{13.4}\]


Quick revision

The analysis must follow the randomisation.
Homogeneous units → CRD; one gradient → RCBD; two gradients → Latin square.
Large plots for one factor → split-plot with two error terms.
Report means with SEm, SEd, CD and CV.
Counts → square root; percentages → angular transformation.



Answers to fill in the blanks

1. control 2. random 3. \((t-1)(r-1)\) 4. two 5. (a) 6. critical difference 7. square-root 8. angular (arcsine)



Solutions to numerical and conceptual questions

\((6-1)(4-1) = 15\).
\((5-1)(5-2) = 12\).
By Equation 13.2, SEd \(= \sqrt{2\times2.5/4} = 1.118\); by Equation 13.3, CD \(= 2.131\times1.118 = 2.38\).
Error (a) \(= (4-1)(3-1) = 6\); error (b) \(= 3(4-1)(5-1) = 36\).

14.1 Learning outcomes
Distinguish Pearson and Spearman correlation, interpret simple and multiple regression coefficients, check model assumptions and influential observations, and evaluate prediction on held-out observations.
crumbs: 14  Correlation and regression for agricultural prediction

title: 14  Correlation and regression for agricultural prediction
section: 14.2 Association is not a treatment effect
text:
14.2 Association is not a treatment effect
Pearson’s correlation measures the strength and direction of a linear relationship between quantitative variables. Spearman’s correlation applies Pearson’s idea to ranks and describes monotonic association. Neither establishes causation, and a value near zero need not imply the absence of a nonlinear relationship. Both can be distorted by pooling unlike groups or by dependence among observations.
The simulated farm_yield.csv contains 100 independent teaching records with nitrogen application, seasonal rainfall, and yield. It is constructed for a regression lesson and is not evidence for a real fertilizer recommendation.

farm <- read.csv("data/farm_yield.csv")
plot(yield_t_ha ~ nitrogen_kg_ha, farm, pch = 19,
     xlab = "Nitrogen (kg/ha)", ylab = "Yield (t/ha)")







cor.test(farm$nitrogen_kg_ha, farm$yield_t_ha, method = "pearson")


    Pearson's product-moment correlation

data:  farm$nitrogen_kg_ha and farm$yield_t_ha

alternative hypothesis: true correlation is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 0.6741515 0.8385662
sample estimates:
      cor 
0.7687722

    Spearman's rank correlation rho

data:  farm$nitrogen_kg_ha and farm$yield_t_ha
S = 40283, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: true rho is not equal to 0
sample estimates:

0.7582784 


Inspect scatter plots before interpreting a correlation coefficient. Pearson’s usual test assumes independent pairs and a suitable bivariate sampling model; ranks do not fix clustering or confounding. Spearman’s test uses an approximation here because rounded measurements can create ties.

title: 14  Correlation and regression for agricultural prediction
text:
14.3 Simple linear regression
The model \(Y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1X_i+\epsilon_i\) describes a conditional mean response. The intercept is the predicted mean when \(X=0\); the slope is a change in mean response per unit increase in \(X\). Least squares minimizes squared residuals. The regression direction matters: a model predicting yield from nitrogen is not interchangeable with one predicting nitrogen from yield.

title: 14  Correlation and regression for agricultural prediction
section: 14.4 Worked calculation: what least squares estimates
text:
14.4 Worked calculation: what least squares estimates
For a simple regression with an intercept, the estimated slope is
\[b_1=\frac{\sum(x_i-\bar{x})(y_i-\bar{y})}{\sum(x_i-\bar{x})^2},\qquad b_0=\bar{y}-b_1\bar{x}.\]
The slope is undefined when every predictor value is identical: the denominator is zero. A range of predictor values is necessary to estimate a relationship. The calculation below verifies the coefficients from lm() rather than treating its output as a black box.

x <- farm$nitrogen_kg_ha
y <- farm$yield_t_ha
b1 <- sum((x - mean(x)) * (y - mean(y))) / sum((x - mean(x))^2)
b0 <- mean(y) - b1 * mean(x)
rbind(manual = c(intercept = b0, slope = b1), lm = unname(coef(simple)))

       intercept      slope
manual  3.077606 0.01831709
lm      3.077606 0.01831709


Residuals are observed minus fitted responses. With an intercept, least squares makes their sum approximately zero. This algebraic property does not show that their errors are independent or normally distributed. Those require design knowledge and diagnostics.

The nitrogen coefficient now describes a change while rainfall is held fixed in the model. It may differ from the simple-regression coefficient because the models ask different questions. Omitted confounders, measurement error, and nonlinearity can still bias interpretation. Adding predictors raises ordinary \(R^2\) even if they contribute little; high \(R^2\) does not establish causality or reliable future prediction.
Strongly correlated predictors make separate coefficients unstable. In the crop trial, treatment and applied nitrogen are closely linked, so including both without thought can make individual effects hard to interpret. Select predictors using scientific reasoning, design, and an evaluation plan rather than repeated p-value searches.

title: 14  Correlation and regression for agricultural prediction
text:
14.6 Residuals, leverage, and influence

old <- par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(multiple)







par(old)
head(sort(cooks.distance(multiple), decreasing = TRUE))

        52         81         74         10         94          3 
0.07415445 0.06520610 0.04821445 0.04345712 0.03896112 0.03604932 


The residual-versus-fitted plot checks mean structure, the Q–Q plot checks the error distribution, the scale-location plot checks spread, and leverage/influence diagnostics identify observations that can strongly affect estimates. Check influential records against source information; do not delete them merely to improve fit. Classical t-tests and intervals need assumptions about errors, including independence and constant variance. Normality concerns the errors for small-sample inference, not every predictor’s marginal distribution.
crumbs: 14  Correlation and regression for agricultural prediction

title: 14  Correlation and regression for agricultural prediction
text:
14.7 Categorical predictors and reference levels
Regression can include categorical variables through indicator coding. A two-variety example illustrates this without requiring the varieties to be interpreted as numeric doses. The reference level determines the intercept’s meaning, while the fitted mean for each observation remains unchanged under a consistent recoding.

trial <- read.csv("data/crop_trial.csv")
trial$variety <- factor(trial$variety, levels = c("A", "B"))
trial$block <- factor(trial$block)
variety_model <- lm(yield_t_ha ~ block + treatment + variety, data = trial)
coef(variety_model)

     (Intercept)           block2           block3           block4 
       3.4150000        0.1941667        0.3391667        0.5725000 
          block5 treatmentControl treatmentMineral         varietyB 
       0.4166667       -0.7125000        0.5190000        0.2340000 


The varietyB coefficient compares B with A conditional on the other terms in this additive model. It assumes a common variety difference across treatments. The preceding ANOVA chapter explains how a treatment-by-variety interaction relaxes that assumption. ANOVA and regression are connected expressions of linear modelling, rather than unrelated procedures selected solely by the appearance of a response column.
crumbs: 14  Correlation and regression for agricultural prediction

title: 14  Correlation and regression for agricultural prediction
section: 14.8 Residual standard error and explained variation
text:
14.8 Residual standard error and explained variation
The residual sum of squares measures unexplained squared deviations after fitting. Dividing by residual degrees of freedom and taking a square root gives the residual standard error, in yield units. \(R^2\) compares residual sum of squares with the total sum of squares around the observed mean:
\[R^2=1-\frac{\sum(y_i-\widehat{y}_i)^2}{\sum(y_i-\bar{y})^2}.\]

rss <- sum(residuals(multiple)^2)
tss <- sum((farm$yield_t_ha - mean(farm$yield_t_ha))^2)
c(manual_R_squared = 1 - rss / tss,
  reported_R_squared = summary(multiple)$r.squared,
  residual_standard_error = sqrt(rss / df.residual(multiple)))

       manual_R_squared      reported_R_squared residual_standard_error 
              0.6888415               0.6888415               0.3469405 


An in-sample \(R^2\) describes fit to the observed response variation under that model. It is not the percentage probability that a prediction is correct. A narrow predictor range can produce a low \(R^2\) even when a small slope is estimated usefully; a common time trend can produce a high \(R^2\) for an unsuitable causal interpretation. Compare models in relation to their purpose and predictor domain.
crumbs: 14  Correlation and regression for agricultural prediction

title: 14  Correlation and regression for agricultural prediction
section: 14.9 Nonlinearity and an apparent fertilizer optimum
text:
14.9 Nonlinearity and an apparent fertilizer optimum
Crop response to a nutrient may increase initially and then approach a plateau or decline. A straight line over a restricted range can approximate part of that response without defining a biological optimum. A quadratic model adds a squared predictor term. In R formulas, write I(x^2) so the power is interpreted arithmetically.

quadratic <- lm(yield_t_ha ~ nitrogen_kg_ha + I(nitrogen_kg_ha^2) + rainfall_mm,
                 data = farm)
summary(quadratic)


Call:
lm(formula = yield_t_ha ~ nitrogen_kg_ha + I(nitrogen_kg_ha^2) + 
    rainfall_mm, data = farm)

Residuals:
     Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
-0.76092 -0.25807  0.02466  0.22923  0.67272 

Coefficients:
                     Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)         2.034e+00  4.050e-01   5.021 2.37e-06 ***
nitrogen_kg_ha      1.660e-02  8.536e-03   1.945   0.0547 .  
I(nitrogen_kg_ha^2) 8.248e-06  5.019e-05   0.164   0.8698    
rainfall_mm         1.730e-03  3.158e-04   5.479 3.44e-07 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 0.3487 on 96 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.6889,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.6792 
F-statistic: 70.87 on 3 and 96 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16


For a concave quadratic \(a+bN+cN^2\) with \(c<0\), its mathematical maximum occurs at \(-b/(2c)\). If c is positive, the stationary point is a minimum, not an optimum. Even a concave fitted curve may place its maximum outside the observed nitrogen range, where it is unsupported extrapolation. The supplied simulation is generated with a linear mean response, so a quadratic term should not be presented as discovering a true fertilizer optimum.
An economic optimum additionally depends on crop price, input cost, and an appropriate response function. A fitted yield curve alone cannot supply those missing quantities. A defensible recommendation also needs replicated evidence across relevant environments and an assessment of uncertainty. In this introductory course, use nonlinear patterns to motivate questions and model checks before offering recommendations.
crumbs: 14  Correlation and regression for agricultural prediction

title: 14  Correlation and regression for agricultural prediction
text:
14.10 Predict and evaluate honestly

new_farm <- data.frame(nitrogen_kg_ha = 80, rainfall_mm = 650)
predict(multiple, new_farm, interval = "confidence")

       fit      lwr      upr
1 4.544382 4.474566 4.614198

predict(multiple, new_farm, interval = "prediction")

       fit      lwr      upr
1 4.544382 3.852271 5.236493

set.seed(531)
train_id <- sample(seq_len(nrow(farm)), size = 75)
train <- farm[train_id, ]
test <- farm[-train_id, ]
fit_train <- lm(yield_t_ha ~ nitrogen_kg_ha + rainfall_mm, data = train)
pred <- predict(fit_train, test)
baseline <- rep(mean(train$yield_t_ha), nrow(test))
data.frame(method = c("Regression", "Training mean"),
           RMSE = c(sqrt(mean((test$yield_t_ha - pred)^2)),
                    sqrt(mean((test$yield_t_ha - baseline)^2))),
           MAE = c(mean(abs(test$yield_t_ha - pred)),
                   mean(abs(test$yield_t_ha - baseline))))

         method      RMSE       MAE
1    Regression 0.3892038 0.3225455
2 Training mean 0.6895416 0.5703840


A confidence interval concerns the mean response at the specified predictors; a prediction interval includes variation in a new observation and is wider. Both rely on the model. Avoid extrapolation outside the training range and consider combinations of predictors that may be unusual even when each is individually within range.
A random holdout is suitable for these independent simulated records. For repeated farms, spatial clusters, or time series, split by group, location, or time as appropriate. Fit preprocessing steps using training data only. One split gives an unstable estimate, so cross-validation may be needed for serious model comparison. The test set should not become another training set through repeated tuning.

text:
14.11 Practical 15 and exercises

Compare Pearson and Spearman coefficients and explain their target relationships.
Interpret the rainfall coefficient and its units. Why is it not automatically a causal rainfall effect?
Compare simple and multiple nitrogen slopes. Explain what changes in their interpretation.
Compare a confidence and prediction interval for the same new record.
Evaluate the held-out model against the training-mean baseline. Identify a realistic setting where a random row split would be inappropriate.

title: 14  Correlation and regression for agricultural prediction
text:
14.12 Live R laboratory

Fit and interpret a yield model
Edit the code, then select Run R. The first run downloads R into your browser and may take a little time. Copy code also lets you use this example in RStudio.
trial <- data.frame(nitrogen = c(0, 20, 40, 60, 80, 100),
                    yield = c(2.0, 2.6, 3.0, 3.7, 3.9, 4.5))
model <- lm(yield ~ nitrogen, data = trial)
summary(model)
predict(model, newdata = data.frame(nitrogen = 50), interval = "prediction")
plot(yield ~ nitrogen, trial, pch = 19, col = "#237f83",
     xlab = "Nitrogen (kg/ha)", ylab = "Simulated yield (t/ha)")
abline(model, col = "#bc7c21", lwd = 2)
Investigate. Interpret the slope with units and distinguish a prediction interval for a new observation from a confidence interval for the mean. Do not extrapolate this simulated linear response to arbitrary doses.

title: 14  Correlation and regression for agricultural prediction
text:
14.13 Chapter Summary

Fill in the blanks
Answers are given at the end of the chapter.

The correlation coefficient lies between __________ and +1.
Spearman’s correlation is based on __________.
In \(y = b_0 + b_1x\), \(b_1\) is the __________.
Least squares minimises the sum of squared __________.
\(R^2\) is the proportion of variation in \(y\) explained by the __________.
In multiple regression a coefficient is interpreted holding other predictors __________.
An observation with unusual \(x\) values has high __________.
Prediction accuracy is best judged on __________ data.



Short-answer questions

Distinguish between correlation and regression.
Why does association not establish a treatment effect?
What are the assumptions of linear regression?
Explain leverage and influence.
Why should prediction be evaluated on data not used to fit the model?



Numerical and conceptual questions
Answers are given at the end of the chapter.

For a data set, \(S_{xy} = 40\), \(S_{xx} = 20\), \(\bar x = 4\) and \(\bar y = 10\). Find the regression line.
A regression has SSE = 30 and total SS = 120. Find \(R^2\).
If \(r = 0.9\) in simple regression, what is \(R^2\)?



Important formulae
Least-squares estimates:
\[
b_1 = \frac{\sum (x_i - \bar x)(y_i - \bar y)}{\sum (x_i - \bar x)^2}, \qquad b_0 = \bar y - b_1 \bar x
\tag{14.1}\]
Coefficient of determination:
\[
R^2 = 1 - \frac{\sum (y_i - \hat y_i)^2}{\sum (y_i - \bar y)^2}
\tag{14.2}\]


Quick revision

Correlation → strength of linear association; regression → prediction of \(y\) from \(x\).
Association ≠ causation.
Check residuals, leverage and influence before trusting a model.
\(R^2\) → explained variation; RSE → typical prediction error.
Evaluate predictions on held-out data.



Answers to fill in the blanks

1. −1 2. ranks 3. slope 4. residuals 5. model 6. constant 7. leverage 8. held-out



Solutions to numerical and conceptual questions

By Equation 14.1, \(b_1 = 40/20 = 2\) and \(b_0 = 10 - 2\times4 = 2\); \(\hat y = 2 + 2x\).
By Equation 14.2, \(R^2 = 1 - 30/120 = 0.75\).
\(R^2 = r^2 = 0.81\).

title: 15  Reproducible reports with R Markdown and Quarto
section: 15.2 A report is an argument supported by evidence
text:
15.2 A report is an argument supported by evidence
A useful report states a question, describes data and design, explains decisions, presents results, and discusses limitations. Embedding R code keeps numerical evidence connected to its computation. If a dataset changes, re-rendering updates the results. This reduces transcription errors but cannot correct an unsuitable analysis.
R Markdown usually uses .Rmd source files and rmarkdown::render(). Quarto uses .qmd source files and the quarto render command. Both can execute R through knitr. Their configuration differs: R Markdown uses output: whereas Quarto uses format:. Simply renaming an old bookdown file is not a complete migration; chapter configuration, references, chunk options, and dependencies need checking.
crumbs: Module 7 · Reproducible research and AI-assisted coding
15  Reproducible reports with R Markdown and Quarto

title: 15  Reproducible reports with R Markdown and Quarto
text:
15.3 Anatomy of a Quarto document
The following is a complete small document. The YAML header defines metadata and formats, ordinary Markdown supplies prose, and the R chunk computes a table. Save it as report.qmd in the project folder. The separate practicals/report.qmd provides a fuller working example.
---
title: "Plant growth: a reproducible analysis"
author: "Student name"
format:
  html: default
  pdf: default
  docx: default
---

# Question

How do dry-weight measurements vary among the documented groups?

::: {#tbl-weight .cell tbl-cap='Mean dry weight by group in PlantGrowth.'}

```{.r .cell-code}
data("PlantGrowth", package = "datasets")
tab <- aggregate(weight ~ group, PlantGrowth, mean)
knitr::kable(tab, digits = 2)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}


|group | weight|
|:-----|------:|
|ctrl  |   5.03|
|trt1  |   4.66|
|trt2  |   5.53|


:::
:::

Interpret the estimates in @tbl-weight using the dataset documentation.
Use descriptive chunk labels; figure labels begin with fig- and table labels with tbl- for cross-references. A figure chunk can use #| fig-cap: "...". A hidden setup chunk may set #| include: false, but keep the source available to readers. echo: false hides code, not results. eval: false displays an example without executing it. Avoid hiding warnings until they have been investigated.

15.4 Dynamic values, figures, and interactive output
Inline R inserts a computed value into a sentence. For example, write the literal source 30 to report the number of observations. This keeps prose synchronized with the data. Do not hard-code a p-value in the discussion while the model updates elsewhere.
Use knitr::kable() for simple portable tables and ordinary R plots for graphics. HTML widgets such as Plotly need an HTML output context. In multi-format documents, test knitr::is_html_output() and use a static plot for PDF and Word, as demonstrated in the visualization chapter.

15.6 Render and share
Run shell commands in the Terminal, not in the R Console:
quarto preview
quarto render --to html
quarto render --to docx
quarto render --to pdf
quarto render practicals/report.qmd --to html
PDF output requires a working LaTeX distribution, for example TinyTeX installed through quarto install tinytex. Install it only if PDF is needed. HTML is the default classroom format in the README instructions. Rendering the entire book to Word or PDF combines chapters into a single document. Opening an HTML file locally is not the same as publishing it to a public server.
Before sharing, restart R and render from source. Include source files, permitted data, metadata, package requirements, and instructions. sessionInfo() records R and loaded package versions. For a stable course release, consider a reviewed renv lockfile; do not claim that a package list alone pins an environment.

title: 15  Reproducible reports with R Markdown and Quarto
text:
15.7 Building the report in stages
Let us develop a report in the same order as an analysis. First create the document with its question, data source, and design, even before the final model is chosen. Then add a data-check section, followed by descriptive tables and figures. Only after examining those results should the methods and model sections be completed. This sequence makes the scientific argument visible rather than hiding it behind a final table of p-values.
An effective data section identifies the observational unit, sample size, variable units, collection period, and treatment or sampling scheme. State how the raw file was obtained and whether permission is needed to share it. In the cleaning section, explain missingness, corrections, and exclusions with their consequences for the analysis. Avoid including personal or confidential identifiers merely because they happen to be in the original spreadsheet.
The methods section should name the response, predictors or factors, model, and assumptions in terms that match the actual code. If the text describes a paired test but the code fits an unpaired test, a successful render has reproduced an inconsistency. Read both parts together. The results section should lead with the size and direction of important effects, followed by uncertainty and evidence. Keep mechanistic explanations and generalization limits in the discussion.

title: 15  Reproducible reports with R Markdown and Quarto
text:
15.8 Managing code chunks and dependencies
Each document is easiest to understand when it can be executed from top to bottom in a new session. The first chunk loads packages and reads inputs. Later chunks depend on those named objects. Avoid loading data by hand into the Environment pane and then assuming they will be available during rendering.


::: {#tbl-treatment-means .cell tbl-cap='Mean simulated grain yield by management treatment.'}

```{.r .cell-code}
means <- trial |>
  group_by(treatment) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean_yield = mean(yield_t_ha), .groups = "drop")
knitr::kable(means, digits = 2)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}


|treatment |  n| mean_yield|
|:---------|--:|----------:|
|Compost   | 20|       3.84|
|Control   | 20|       3.12|
|Mineral   | 20|       4.36|


:::
:::
The setup chunk is hidden in the displayed report but remains in the source. It does not install packages. The table chunk visibly records the summary operation. A future reader can distinguish a count of plot records from an estimate of mean yield and can rerun both.
Caching and freezing can save time in large projects, but they can also leave stale output when dependencies are misunderstood. During textbook revision, this project uses freeze: false so examples are executed again. Do not use old cached results to claim that revised code has been checked. For serious projects, record the environment and consider a lockfile, while recognizing that external data sources can change independently of package versions.

title: 15  Reproducible reports with R Markdown and Quarto
text:
15.9 Tables, figures, and numerical precision
A table title should say what was measured, how observations were grouped, and what the numbers represent. Put units in column headings where possible. Report enough digits for interpretation without suggesting unrealistic measurement precision. A yield measured to 0.01 t/ha should not normally be presented to eight decimal places merely because R printed them.
A figure caption should allow the graph to be understood away from the surrounding paragraph. Distinguish observed points from fitted lines, and describe error bars or shaded intervals precisely. “Error bars” is insufficient: are they SD, SE, confidence intervals, or prediction intervals? If an interactive figure permits hovering, retain axis labels and a caption so the static version remains meaningful.
Cross-references are preferable to manually typed numbers. After inserting a new table, @tbl-treatment-means updates its reference automatically. Manually writing “Table 3” can become wrong after reorganization. The same applies to chapter references and figure references. The final review should include checking that a referenced object actually supports the claim made in the sentence.
